15.s:
With reference to RFID Technology, consider the following statements:
I. Passive RFID tags are powered by an internal circuit and utilize it to send response to the reader.
II. Semi-passive RFID tags comprise an internal circuit with power source but rely on radio waves received from the reader to transmit the response.
III. Active RFID tags acquire their power from the readers ' incoming radio waves.
IV. RFID Technology can scan a tag as long as it is within frequency range and it does not have any line-of-sight limitations.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
15.x: I is wrong: passive tags have no battery and are powered by the reader's field. III is wrong: active tags carry their own battery. II (semi-passive: battery runs the chip, reply uses reader's waves) and IV (no line-of-sight needed) are correct.

15.s: Which of the following is NOT correct regarding IoT and AI?
o: IoT devices collect and exchange data through sensors
A smart thermostat is an example of AI rather than IoT
AI analyses data, recognises patterns and makes decisions
Chatbots and image recognition are examples of AI
15.x: A smart thermostat is listed as an IoT example, not an AI example.
xa: IoT is **rule-based, limited learning**; AI uses **machine and deep learning**.
A **fitness wearable** is another IoT example.

15.s: What does the Internet of Things (IoT) refer to?
o: A network limited to industrial robots
Only computers connected through wired networks
A system in which data can be exchanged only after manual approval
Devices with sensors linked in a network and exchanging data without human intervention
15.x: IoT consists of sensor-equipped devices connected through networks that exchange data without human intervention.
15.tq: Select the precise definition and reject restrictive qualifiers such as ‘only’.
xs: **IoT** = **devices with sensors linked in a network, exchanging data without human intervention** — so option **(4)** is correct.
This definition was asked in APPSC **2023** and **2024**.
xa: IoT three-layer model: **perception** (sensors, RFID) → **network** → **application**.
The **mMTC** slice of **5G** serves dense IoT sensors.
IoT applications: smart farming, smart homes, **smart grids**, healthcare, logistics, smart cities.

15.s: Which policy covers 5G, the Internet of Things (IoT) and machine-to-machine (M2M) communication?
15.x: The National Digital Communications Policy (NDCP) 2018 covers 5G, IoT and M2M. The Drone Rules 2021 govern drones, the IT Rules 2021 regulate intermediaries and digital media, and the E-Commerce Rules 2020 protect online consumers.
xs: **NDCP 2018** (National Digital Communications Policy) covers **5G, IoT and M2M** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Drone Rules, 2021** set drone weight classes; they do not cover 5G or IoT.
xa: The **mMTC** slice of 5G serves dense IoT sensors.
IoT is also part of **Digital India**.
MeitY-NASSCOM **IoT CoEs** include **Visakhapatnam**.

15.s: Which of the following correctly represents the three-layer model of the Internet of Things, from the device-facing layer to the user-facing layer?
15.x: The three-layer IoT model consists of the perception layer, network layer and application layer. The perception layer senses, the network layer transmits and the application layer provides smart services.
15.tq: Recall the ordered layers and their functional progression.
xs: The three layers are **perception, network, application** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Perception**: sensors, **RFID**; **network**: transmission; **application**: smart services.
xa: Variants: **IIoT** (industrial automation), **IoNT** (nano-devices), Internet of Mobile Things, mission-critical IoT (military).
IoT is **rule-based** with limited learning; **AI** uses machine and deep learning.

15.s: Where are the IoT Centres of Excellence set up through the MeitY-NASSCOM initiative located?
15.x: The MeitY-NASSCOM IoT Centres of Excellence are located at Bengaluru, Gurugram, Gandhinagar and Visakhapatnam.
15.tq: Check the complete location list rather than identifying only one familiar city.
xs: The **MeitY-NASSCOM** IoT CoEs are at **Bengaluru, Gurugram, Gandhinagar and Visakhapatnam** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Hyderabad** hosts the **IMAGE CoE**, not an IoT CoE.
xa: ⚠ IoT CoEs include **Visakhapatnam**; **IMAGE** = Hyderabad; **VARCoE** = **IIT Bhubaneswar**.
Efftronics + **JNTU Kakinada** launched an industry-sponsored **M.Tech in IoT** (Jul 2026).
**Digital India** includes IoT; **NDCP 2018** covers 5G, IoT and M2M.

15.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?

Assembly lines and mass production belong to **Industry 2.0**.
**Mission-critical IoT** = military; **IIoT** = industrial automation; **IoNT** = nano-devices — all correct.
xa: IoT layers: **perception, network, application**.
IoT examples: **smart thermostat**, **fitness wearable**.

15.s: Which IoT variant is concerned with nano-devices?
15.x: IoNT is the Internet of Nano Things; IIoT is industrial automation and mission-critical IoT is military.

15.x: The four-stage version is perception, transport, network and application.

15.x: IoT applications include smart farming, smart homes, smart grids, healthcare, logistics and smart cities.

15.x: A smart thermostat is IoT and IIoT is industrial; the Internet of Mobile Things concerns mobile objects, not assembly lines.

15.x: Wearables such as smartwatches and fitness bands track health indicators and act as IoT end-devices.

15.s: A semi-passive RFID tag differs from an active RFID tag because the semi-passive tag:
o: Uses its battery to run the chip but uses the reader’s field to reply
Has no internal power and cannot contain identity data
Has an independent transmitter and broadcasts over a long range
Uses only a satellite signal for communication
15.x: A semi-passive tag’s battery powers its chip, but it still uses the reader’s field to send its response. An active tag has its own battery and transmitter.
15.tq: Focus on the exact distinction between battery use and transmission capability.
xs: A **semi-passive** tag's **battery runs the chip only**; it **uses the reader's field to reply** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Having an independent **transmitter** and broadcasting over long range describes an **active** tag.
xa: **Passive** tags have **no internal battery** and backscatter the reader's signal.
⚠ Trap: passive tags are **not** powered by an internal circuit (APPSC-G1 **2022**).
RFID sits in the **perception** layer of IoT.

15.s: What is an RFID tag that has its own battery and transmitter called?
15.x: An active tag has its own battery and transmitter; a passive tag has no battery and backscatters the reader's signal.
xa: ⚠ This is the **APPSC-G1 2022** trap (key: **II and IV only**).
**Semi-passive**: battery runs the chip only; still replies via the reader's field.
Passive tags are **cheap, short range**; active tags broadcast over **long range**.

15.s: How does a passive RFID tag reply to the reader?
o: Using a battery that runs a transmitter
Using a battery that runs the chip only
15.x: Passive tags have no battery and backscatter the reader's signal; active tags broadcast with their own transmitter.

15.s: 'eVTOL Technology' is related to which field ?

DGCA training institutes for flight certification

19.s:
With reference to " Blockchain Technology”, consider the following statements:
I. It is a public ledger that everyone can inspect, but no single user controls.
II. The structure and design of blockchain is such that all the data in it are about cryptocurrency only.
III. Applications that depend on basic features of blockchain can be developed without. anybody's permission.

19.x: I is right: a public ledger anyone can inspect but no single user controls. III is right: blockchain apps can be built without permission. II is wrong: blockchain holds land records, certificates, supply chains and more, not only cryptocurrency.

19.s: Which of the following describes a blockchain?
o: A centralised database controlled exclusively by a central bank
A time-stamped series of immutable records managed by a cluster of computers not owned by one entity
A password-protected database maintained by a single administrator
A temporary record of transactions stored only on users' devices
19.x: A blockchain is a time-stamped series of immutable records managed by a cluster of computers rather than a single owner.
19.tq: Use the precise definition and eliminate centralised-database distractors.
xs: A blockchain is a **time-stamped series of immutable records** managed by a **cluster of computers not owned by any single entity** — option **(2)** is correct (APPSC **2018** definition).
It is not centralised: there is **no central validator** and no single administrator, so options (1) and (3) are wrong.
Records are not temporary — they are **immutable** and copies sit with participants, so option (4) fails.
xa: Records are **visible to relevant stakeholders without risk of alteration**; database copies sit with participants (UPSC **2020**).
**Bitcoin (2009)** was the first cryptocurrency and the **first use of blockchain**, created by pseudonymous **Satoshi Nakamoto**.
Each **block** holds transaction details, the **hash of the previous block** and a **timestamp**.

19.s: Why can stakeholders view the records of a blockchain but not alter them?
o: The database is deleted after each transaction
A single administrator edits every copy
Stakeholders hold copies and changes need consensus
Only the data-entry operator keeps a copy
19.x: Replicated copies held by stakeholders and the need for consensus protect records from unauthorised alteration.
xa: Notes: records are visible to relevant stakeholders **without risk of alteration**; database copies sit with participants (UPSC **2020**, **2026**).
**Hash**: changing data changes the hash, so **tampering shows**.
**Distributed ledger**: a **single source of truth** with no central validator.

19.s: What is a shared ledger copied across many nodes, working as a single source of truth without a central validator, called?
19.x: A distributed ledger is a shared ledger replicated across many nodes without a central validator.
19.tq: Match the exact technical term with its defining function.
xs: A shared ledger copied at many **nodes** and acting as a **"single source of truth"** with no central validator is a **distributed ledger** — option **(4)**.
A **hash** is a cryptographic fingerprint of data; a **smart contract** is self-executing code on a blockchain — neither is the ledger itself.
xa: **Node** = a computer holding a copy of the ledger.
**Consensus** = the rule by which nodes agree on valid transactions.
**Immutability** = once recorded, data is nearly impossible to alter **without consensus**.

19.s: Besides transaction details and a timestamp, what does a block of a blockchain ordinarily contain?
o: The private key of every participant
A copy of every earlier block
The hash of the previous block
19.x: A block holds transaction details, the previous block's hash and a timestamp, not participants' private keys.
xa: The **hash** link to the previous block means changing any data changes the hash, so **tampering shows**.
**Immutability**: recorded data is nearly impossible to alter without **consensus**.
Bitcoin features: **public/private keys and wallets**; **mining** validates transactions.

19.s: Which of the following is NOT correct regarding blockchain terms?
o: A hash is a cryptographic fingerprint whose change reveals tampering
A blockchain has no central validator
A node is a computer holding a copy of the ledger
Immutability means only a central authority can modify recorded data
19.x: Immutability means recorded data is nearly impossible to alter without consensus; there is no central validator.
xa: **Distributed ledger**: shared ledger copied at many nodes, a **"single source of truth"**.
**Consensus**: the rule by which nodes agree on valid transactions.
A **block** holds transaction details + **hash of the previous block** + **timestamp**.

n: Radio waves have wavelengths greater than 1 metre. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 81-86]
Microwaves have wavelengths from 1 millimetre to 1 metre. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 81-86]
Infrared waves have wavelengths from 700 nanometres to 1 millimetre. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 81-86]
Ultraviolet waves have wavelengths from 10 to 400 nanometres. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 81-86]
xa: **Visible light:** **400 to 700 nanometres**.
**X-rays:** **0.01 to 10 nanometres**.
**Gamma rays:** less than **0.01 nanometre**.

20.s: Which waves are mainly used in radar and satellite communication?
20.x: Microwaves serve satellites, radar and 5G; UV, X-rays and gamma rays are ionising and not used for normal communication.
n: Radio waves are used for radio, television, mobile communication, Wi-Fi, and Bluetooth. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 57-64]
Microwaves are used for satellite communication, radar, 5G, and microwave links. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 57-64]
Ultraviolet, X-ray, and gamma radiation are not used for normal communication. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 57-64]
xa: **Infrared** is used in **remote controls** and **short-range data communication**.
**Visible light** is used experimentally in **Li-Fi**.
**Li-Fi** does **not pass through walls**; **Wi-Fi** does.

20.s: Which of the following pairs (radiation – use) is correctly matched?

Infrared radiation is used in remote controls and short-range data communication. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 57-64]
Visible light is used experimentally in Li-Fi and in some optical fibres. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 57-64]
xa: **Radio waves** also carry **Wi-Fi** and **Bluetooth**.

**Microwaves** serve **radar** and **5G**.

20.s: Optical fibres, though bent in any manner, allows light to pass through. What is the inference that one can draw from it?

Light can flow through the optical fibres.
Light can travel through the fibres because of their ductility.
Light can travel through the fibres due to multiple total internal reflection.
20.x: Light stays inside a bent fibre because it undergoes repeated total internal reflections; ductility has nothing to do with it, and light still travels straight between reflections.

20.s: In total internal reflection, the light travels from
o: rarer to denser medium and it occurs with no loss of intensity.
denser to rarer medium and it occurs with no loss of intensity.
rarer to denser medium and it occurs with loss of intensity.
denser to rarer medium and it occurs with loss of intensity.
20.x: TIR occurs when light goes from a denser to a rarer medium above the critical angle, and the whole of the light is reflected back, with no loss of intensity.

20.s: Light rays move in straight lines. But through an optical fibre, they can move in any type of zig-zag path because
o: the holes through the fibres are extremely fine.
light rays are absorbed at the entry end and relieved at the exit end of the fibre.
scattering of light occurs inside the fibre.
successive total internal reflections occur as a ray moves through the fibre.
20.x: Successive total internal reflections at the core boundary give the zig-zag path through the fibre.

20.s: Brilliance of diamond is due to
20.x: Diamond's very high refractive index gives a small critical angle (~24.4°), so light inside it suffers multiple total internal reflections, which causes its brilliance.

28.x: A responsible digital citizen identifies misinformation, verifies sources, protects personal data, respects privacy and participates in civil discourse.
28.tq: Choose the behaviour that combines verification with responsible digital participation.
xs: A responsible digital citizen is marked by **identifying misinformation and verifying sources** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The citizen also **protects personal data**, so disclosing it is wrong, and engages in **civil discourse** rather than withdrawing.
Forwarding everything is the risk: **one misleading forward** → panic, violence or reputational damage.
xa: Rights side: **online grievance redressal**, **e-consultations**, **open government data**.
AP example: **Grama and Ward Sachivalayam** system.

28.s: Which of the following is a responsibility of a digital citizen?
28.x: A low digital footprint, civil discourse and not sharing unverified content are responsibilities; the other three are rights-side aspects.

28.s: The Digital Detox initiative of the Karnataka Government was undertaken with which organisation and focused on which area?
o: I4C; takedown notices and court orders
28.x: The Karnataka Government's Digital Detox initiative was undertaken with the All India Game Developers Forum and addressed gaming and social-media use.
28.tq: Match the initiative with its partner organisation and subject area.
xs: Karnataka's **Digital Detox** was done with **AIGDF** (All India Game Developers Forum) on **gaming and social-media use** — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-G2 **2025** PYQ).
**PIB FCU** debunks government-related fake news; **I4C** runs **SAHYOG** takedowns.
xa: WHO lists **Gaming Disorder** in **ICD-11**.
**UK** announced a social-media ban for **under-16s**.

29.s: Computer viruses can infect
29.x: Viruses infect stored files, so a storage device such as a pen drive can carry them; display, keyboard and network card hold no files.

29.s: What is the term for malicious software designed to disrupt, damage, or gain unauthorized access to a computer system?
29.src: APPSC Forest Range Officer Mains Paper-I General Studies & M
29.x: Of the options only 'virus' is malicious software; bacteria, Plasmodium and parasites are biological.

29.s: Which of the following is NOT a computer virus?
29.x: Webroot is an antivirus product; rootkits, trojans and bots are malware.

29.s: A fault in a computer program which prevents it from working correctly is known as
29.src: Grama Ward Sachivalayam Category-II(A) Engg. Asst./Ward Amen
29.x: A bug is a fault in a program that stops it working correctly; phishing and spam are attacks, booting is starting a computer.

29.s: Computer Virus is called
29.src: Jr. Accounts, Asst. Engineers in AP Municipalities 2012
29.x: Printed key: a computer virus is loosely called a 'bug'; strictly a bug is a program fault, but bit, byte and PROM are clearly wrong.

29.s: Which of the following is NOT antivirus software ?
29.x: A rootkit is malware that hides other malware; McAfee, Kaspersky and Avast are antivirus software.

29.s: A form of virus explicitly designed to hide itself from detection by antivirus software is called as
29.x: A stealth virus hides itself from antivirus detection; a boot-sector virus infects the boot record and a metamorphic virus rewrites its code.

29.s: VIRUS stands for
29.x: VIRUS is expanded as Vital Information Resource(s) Under Siege.

29.s: Single-word reference to viruses, worms etc. is
29.x: Malware (malicious software) is the single word covering viruses, worms, trojans and the like.

29.s: In the field of computer, VIRUS stands for
29.x: VIRUS = Vital Information Resource Under Siege.

29.s: An intentionally disruptive software that spreads from computer to computer is known as :
29.x: A virus is disruptive software that replicates and spreads from computer to computer; search engines, chat and e-mail are not malicious.

29.s: A malware, that looks like a legitimate software and once it tricks a user into installing it, acts pretty much like a virus or worm, is known as :
29.x: A Trojan looks like legitimate software, tricks the user into installing it and then acts like a virus or worm.

29.s: A computer virus is –
o: A computer program that can replicate itself
A virus that affects health of human being
29.x: A computer virus is a program that can replicate itself; it does not affect human health.

29.s: Viruses can enter to computer as an attachment of
29.x: Viruses can arrive attached to images, audio/video files and downloads – all of these.

29.s: What are the types of malware?
29.x: Worms are a malware type; caterpillars and lions are not, and 'horses' is not the term (Trojan horse is).

29.s: Which one of the following is a set of program instruction that can attach itself to a file, reproduces itself and spread to other file?
29.x: A virus attaches itself to a file, reproduces and spreads to other files; a worm spreads without attaching and a trojan does not replicate.

29.s: Which one of the following is the malicious program that allows the concealment of that program by modifying the host’s operating system so that the malware is hidden from the user?
29.x: A rootkit modifies the host's operating system to conceal itself and other malware.

29.s:
Consider the following statements.

I. Malware is the defective software and has contained harmful bugs.

II. Rootkits, computer viruses, worms, trojan horses and spyware are some important malwares.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x: Statement I is wrong: malware is designed to harm, not just defective software with bugs. Statement II is right: rootkits, viruses, worms, trojans and spyware are malware.

29.s:
Consider the following statements.

I. Computer worm uses a computer network to send copies of itself to other nodes without any user intervention.

II. Like a virus, worm needs to attach itself to an existing program.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x: A worm sends copies of itself across a network without user action (I correct), and unlike a virus it need not attach to a program (II wrong).

29.s: Which of the following is a threat for electronic payment systems?
29.src: Grama Ward Sachivalayam Category-III Village Agriculture Ass
29.x: Viruses, worms and trojans all threaten electronic payment systems, so 'all of the above'.

29.s: Who is known as the 'Father of Computer Virology'?
29.src: APPSC Degree Lecturers General Studies & Mental Ability 2020
29.x: John von Neumann's 1949 theory of self-reproducing automata underlies computer viruses, so he is called the father of computer virology; Ivanovsky and Beijerinck founded biological virology.

29.s: Which malware attaches to files and generally needs the user to run the infected file?
29.x: A virus attaches to files or programmes and usually needs the user to execute the infected file; a worm spreads without user interaction.
xa: A virus **corrupts/deletes data**.
⚠ **Virus** = user must run it; **Worm** = spreads without user interaction.
APPSC **2024** key gave **Virus** for the malware definition.

29.s: A malicious programme is disguised as legitimate software, does not self-replicate and opens a backdoor into a system. What is it called?
29.x: A Trojan is disguised as legitimate software, does not self-replicate and may open a backdoor for unauthorised access.
29.tq: Apply the three-part distinction of disguise, self-replication and backdoor access.
xs: Disguised as legitimate software, **no self-replication**, opens **backdoors** = **Trojan** — so option **(4)** is correct.
A **worm** self-replicates; a **virus** attaches to files; a **rootkit** hides other malware.
xa: Example: **Zeus Trojan**; CERT-In flagged the **Dyreza Trojan** (**2014**).
Exam angle: "no self-replication, disguised" = **trojan**.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about a computer worm:
1. A worm can self-replicate and spread across networks.
2. A worm requires the user to execute an infected file before it spreads.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x: Worms self-replicate across networks without user interaction; needing the user to run an infected file describes a virus.

29.s: What is malware that shows unwanted ads and comes bundled with free or pirated software called?
29.x: Adware shows unwanted ads bundled with free/pirated software; encrypting files for ransom is ransomware.
xa: Examples: spyware **Pegasus**, adware **Fireball**, keylogger **DarkHotel**.
Adware comes bundled with **free/pirated software**.

29.s: Which of the following is the principal feature of a rootkit?
o: It spreads only through infected removable files
It sends repeated advertising messages to users
It demands ransom in cryptocurrency after encrypting files
It obtains administrator-level access and hides other malware
29.x: A rootkit gains deep administrator-level access and conceals other malicious components, making it particularly difficult to detect.
29.tq: Identify the defining privilege and concealment feature of the malware.
xs: A rootkit **obtains administrator-level access and hides other malware** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is the **hardest to detect** malware type.
Ads = **adware**; ransom for encrypted files = **ransomware**.
xa: Example: **Stuxnet** components.
⚠ **Rootkit** = hides other malware; **Keylogger** = records keystrokes.

29.s: What type of malware is Mirai, known for massive DDoS attacks using hijacked IoT devices?
29.x: Mirai is a botnet that hijacked IoT devices and used them to launch large-scale DDoS attacks.
xa: **DDoS** floods a server from many machines so genuine users are denied service.
Botnets are also used for **spam** and **crypto-mining**.

29.s: Which malware records keystrokes such as passwords, PINs and OTPs?
29.x: A keylogger records keystrokes; a rootkit hides other malware.

29.s: Which malware encrypts a victim's files and demands payment, often in cryptocurrency?
29.x: Ransomware encrypts files and demands a ransom, as in the AIIMS Delhi attack (2022).

29.s: What does spyware mainly do?
o: Carries out secret surveillance and steals passwords or banking data
Hides other malware with administrator access
29.x: Spyware secretly watches users and steals data, e.g. Pegasus; unwanted ads are adware.

29.s: What is the full form of VIRUS?
29.x: VIRUS stands for Vital Information Resources Under Siege; it is a program that can copy itself and spread.

29.s: What type of malware is Zeus?
29.x: Zeus is a Trojan: it is disguised as genuine software, does not self-replicate and opens a backdoor.

29.s: Fireball is an example of which type of malware?
29.x: Fireball is adware, which shows unwanted ads and comes bundled with free or pirated software.

29.s: First computer virus is known as
29.src: APPSC Assistant Motor Vehicle Inspectors, Agriculture Office
29.x: Creeper (1971, Bob Thomas, ARPANET) is regarded as the first computer virus.

29.s: What is the name of the virus that recently paralysed computers and networks in various countries?
29.x: WannaCry (May 2017) ransomware paralysed computers and networks in about 150 countries.

29.s: The Union Home Ministry has issued an alert to all states warning them about the vulnerability in the Android operating system that allows malware applications to pose as legitimate apps and access user data of all kind. What is the name of this malware?
29.src: APPSC Polytechnic Lecturers (S1) General Studies & Mental Ab
29.x: StrandHogg is the Android vulnerability that lets malware pose as legitimate apps; Zeus, SpyEye and Shylock are banking trojans.

29.s: Which was the first computer virus that was created by two brothers from Pakistan?
29.x: Brain (1986) was written by the Alvi brothers of Lahore, Pakistan.

29.s: The first computer virus is known as―
29.x: Creeper (1971) is the first computer virus; ILOVEYOU, Melissa and the Morris worm came later.

29.s: The first computer virus is known as
29.x: Creeper (1971) is the first virus; Elk Cloner (1982) was only the first found in the wild.

29.s: The terms 'Petya' and 'WannaCry' are related to
29.x: Petya and WannaCry are ransomware attacks (2016-17).

29.s: The terms 'WannaCry, Petya, Eternal Blue' sometimes mentioned news recently are related to
29.x: WannaCry and Petya are ransomware and EternalBlue the Windows exploit WannaCry used, so all relate to cyber attacks (UPSC 2018 key c).

29.s: In which country, the Pegasus spyware has been developed?
29.x: Pegasus spyware was developed by Israel's NSO Group.

29.s: The terms 'WannaCry, Petya and EternalBlue' sometimes mentioned in the news recently are related to :
29.x: WannaCry, Petya and EternalBlue relate to cyberattacks (ransomware and its exploit).

29.s: One of the first viruses to attract widespread public attention was designed to infect MS-DOS on 6th March 1992. Name of the virus is –
29.x: Michelangelo was set to strike MS-DOS systems on 6 March 1992 (Michelangelo's birthday); it was first found in 1991.

29.s: ‘Stuxnet’ worm detected in the computers of Iran is –
o: A Hardware to speed up internet working
A malicious program to sabotage nuclear centrifuges
29.x: Stuxnet was a malicious worm built to sabotage Iran's uranium-enrichment centrifuges.

29.s: What is the name of first computer virus?
29.x: Creeper (1971) is regarded as the first computer virus; PARAM is an Indian supercomputer.

29.s: What is the name of the latest virus which caused serious damage to the computer networks of World?
29.src: APPSC Group-III Panchayat Secretary Mains Paper-I General St
29.x:
'latest virus' held only in 2017 — now many later ransomware attacks have followed, e.g. LockBit (general knowledge, not checked)
Asked in 2017: Petya/NotPetya (June 2017), which followed WannaCry (May 2017), was then the latest ransomware (now many later ransomware attacks).

29.s: What was WannaCry (2017)?
o: Ransomware that spread as a worm
29.x: WannaCry was a ransomware worm using EternalBlue, developed by the US NSA; NSO Group made Pegasus spyware.
xa: WannaCry is attributed to **North Korea's Lazarus group**.
EternalBlue exploits a **Windows SMB** flaw.

29.s: Where did Brain (1986), the first IBM-PC boot-sector virus, originate?
29.x: Brain came from Lahore, Pakistan. Creeper (1971) was the first self-replicating program, and Elk Cloner infected Apple II computers.
xa: ⚠ **Creeper** = first virus; **Elk Cloner** = first "in the wild"; **Brain** = first IBM-PC virus.
**Reaper** removed Creeper.
**Petya** and **WannaCry** are **ransomware** (**APPSC-G2 2025**).

29.s: Which computer did Elk Cloner (1982), the first virus found 'in the wild', infect?
29.x: Elk Cloner (1982) was the first virus in the wild, on the Apple II; Brain was the first IBM-PC virus.

29.s: StrandHogg (2019), in which malware poses as genuine apps, is a vulnerability of which platform?
29.x: StrandHogg is an Android vulnerability found by Promon; Windows SMB was the flaw used by EternalBlue.

29.s: Who developed the EternalBlue exploit used by WannaCry?
29.x: EternalBlue was developed by the US NSA and leaked by the Shadow Brokers in 2017; WannaCry is attributed to Lazarus.

29.s: What does the Petya ransomware encrypt?
29.x: Petya (2016) encrypts the master boot record; NotPetya (2017) hit Ukraine.

29.s: Why is Stuxnet notable?
o: Hijacked IoT devices to conduct DDoS attacks
Encrypted files on the computers of AIIMS Delhi
Targeted Iran’s Natanz uranium centrifuges using a worm with rootkit components
Affected Apple II computers as the first virus in the wild
29.x: Stuxnet was a worm containing rootkit components that sabotaged Siemens PLC-controlled uranium centrifuges at Iran’s Natanz facility.
29.tq: Connect the named malware with its distinctive target and industrial-control context.
xs: **Stuxnet** (**2010**) **targeted Iran's Natanz uranium centrifuges using a worm with rootkit components** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It attacked **Siemens PLCs** to sabotage **Iran's nuclear programme**.
IoT DDoS = **Mirai**; AIIMS Delhi = **ransomware**; Apple II = **Elk Cloner**.
xa: Rootkit = deep admin-level access, **hides** other malware.
Cyber espionage is **often state-sponsored** and uses **zero-days**.

29.s: With whom is Pegasus, a zero-click spyware, associated?
o: The NSA of the United States
29.x: Pegasus is state-grade zero-click spyware associated with Israel's NSO Group that can exploit zero-days without user interaction.
xa: **Spyware** secretly monitors users and steals passwords/banking data.
**Zero-day** = flaw developers have had "zero days" to fix.

29.s: Which program was written to remove Creeper, the first self-copying program on ARPANET?
29.x: Creeper (1971) ran on ARPANET; a program called Reaper was made to remove it.

29.s: On which network did Creeper, the first computer virus (1971), appear?
29.x: Creeper, written by Bob Thomas of BBN in 1971, was a self-copying program on ARPANET.

29.s: In which country was the Michelangelo virus first found in 1991?
29.x: Michelangelo, made to infect MS-DOS on 6 March 1992, was first found in Australia in 1991.

29.s: To which group is the WannaCry ransomware attack (May 2017) attributed?
29.x: WannaCry, which used the EternalBlue exploit, is attributed to North Korea's Lazarus group.

29.s: Who created Creeper (1971), the first self-copying program?
29.x: Creeper was written by Bob Thomas of BBN on ARPANET and was removed by Reaper.

29.s: Who wrote Elk Cloner (1982), the first virus found 'in the wild'?
29.x: Elk Cloner, which infected Apple II computers, was written by Rich Skrenta.

29.s: Who created Brain (1986), the first IBM-PC boot-sector virus?
29.x: Brain was created by the Alvi brothers of Lahore, Pakistan.

29.s: Which firm found the StrandHogg Android vulnerability in 2019?
29.x: StrandHogg, in which malware poses as genuine apps, was found by the Norwegian firm Promon.

29.s: Which group leaked the EternalBlue exploit in 2017?
29.x: EternalBlue was developed by the US NSA and leaked by the Shadow Brokers in 2017.

29.s: Which country was hit by the NotPetya attack of 2017?
29.x: NotPetya (2017), a ransomware that encrypts the master boot record, hit Ukraine.

29.s: An attempt to harm, damage or cause threat to a computer system or network is broadly termed as
29.src: Grama Ward Sachivalayam Category-III ANM/Ward Health Secreta
29.x: An attempt to harm, damage or threaten a computer system or network is a cyber attack; cyber bullying targets people.

29.s:
With the growth of cyber technologies, many cases of cyber crimes are reported. Match each cyber threat with its correct description:
Cyber Threat:
A. Hacking
B. Phishing
C. Ransomware
Description:
1. Fraudulent attempts to obtain sensitive information
2. Malicious software that locks data and demands payment
3. Unauthorized access to or manipulation of data
29.src: APPSC Assistant Statistical Officer & Other Posts General St
29.x: Hacking = unauthorised access or manipulation (3), phishing = fraudulent attempt to obtain sensitive information (1), ransomware = locks data and demands payment (2).

29.s: DOS is a form of cyber attack. It prevents the actual user from accessing their own data. DOS stands for
29.src: Grama Ward Sachivalayam Category-I Village Horticulture Assi
29.x: DoS = Denial of Service: the attack stops genuine users from reaching their own data or service.

29.s: Exploiting human elements to gain access to unauthorized resources is called
29.x: Social engineering exploits the human element (trust, urgency) to gain unauthorised access; reverse engineering analyses a product.

29.s: The process through which user data is stolen by illegitimate website that pretends to be a legitimate website is
29.x: A fake website posing as a legitimate one to steal user data is website spoofing; sniffing captures network packets and war dialing scans phone lines.

29.s: Sending message saying that the account is about to be suspended unless the card details and PIN are disclosed immediately is the type of attack
29.x: A message threatening account suspension unless card details and PIN are disclosed is phishing.

29.s: Junk e-mail is also called –
29.x: Junk e-mail is spam.

29.s: A _____ attack comes in the form of deceptive emails or text messages that may ask you to install software or divulge personal information :
29.x: Phishing uses deceptive e-mails or texts asking you to install software or reveal personal information.

29.s: What is Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack?
29.x: A DDoS attack is a cyber attack: a server is flooded with traffic from many compromised machines (botnets).

29.s: An e-mail that appears to originate from one source but actually has been sent from another :
29.x: An e-mail that appears to come from one source but is sent from another is spoofing.

29.s: Which of the following is a type of cyber attack that involves tricking users into revealing sensitive information?
29.x: Phishing tricks users into revealing sensitive information; SQL injection targets databases and DoS floods servers.

29.s: When customers of a Website are unable to access it due to flooding of fake network traffic, it is known as
29.x: Flooding a website with fake traffic so customers cannot reach it is a denial-of-service attack.

29.s: In Cyber Law terminology 'DOS' means :
29.x: In cyber-law terminology DOS means Denial of Service, not Disk Operating System.

29.s: Sending an identical e-mail message repeatedly to a particular address by any abuser is called :
29.x: Sending an identical e-mail repeatedly to one address is e-mail bombing; spamming is bulk mail to many people.

29.s: Which of the following acronyms is normally used to describe unsolicited junk e-mails?
29.x: SPAM describes unsolicited junk e-mail.

29.s: Spam is related to
29.x: Spam (junk e-mail) is a computer term.

29.s: The SolarWinds incident (2020) is an example of which type of attack?
29.x: SolarWinds (2020) is a supply-chain attack; Pegasus is cited as an example of a zero-day exploit.
xa: **Pegasus** is **zero-click spyware** by **NSO Group** (Israel).
**Phishing** = deceptive emails/messages; **vishing** = voice calls.
**DDoS** uses a **botnet** (e.g. **Mirai**).

29.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: Spam – Flooding an inbox to crash it
Man-in-the-middle – Secretly intercepting communication between two parties
E-mail bombing – Malicious database code entered through input fields
29.x: Man-in-the-middle means secretly intercepting or altering communication between two parties. Spam is unsolicited bulk mail, e-mail bombing floods an inbox, and SQL injection inserts malicious database code.
xa: **Spoofing** = faking a sender identity (email ID, caller ID, IP address).
**Vishing** = phishing by voice calls.

29.s:
Consider the following statements about cyber threats:
1. Vishing is malicious database code entered through input fields.
2. Phishing uses deceptive messages posing as a legitimate sender.
3. Spoofing fakes a sender identity such as an e-mail ID or caller ID.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
29.x: Phishing and spoofing are correctly described; vishing is phishing by voice calls, while database code through input fields is SQL injection.

29.s: What is manipulating people through trust, urgency or curiosity to make them take an intended action called?
29.x: Social engineering targets human behaviour, manipulating trust, urgency or curiosity; it can also be AI-enabled.
xa: **Phishing** and **digital arrest** scams rely on social engineering.
Current: **AI-enabled phishing** on Instagram accounts.

29.s: What is an attack that exploits an unknown, unpatched software flaw called?
29.x: A zero-day exploits an unknown, unpatched flaw, as Pegasus does.

29.s: What is phishing carried out through voice calls called?
29.x: Vishing is phishing by voice calls.

29.s: What is an attack that secretly intercepts or alters communication between two parties called?
29.x: Man-in-the-middle secretly intercepts or alters communication between two parties.

29.s: What is a DoS attack?
o: Flooding a server with fake traffic so that genuine users cannot use it
Stealing a person's identity to open bank accounts
Sending junk e-mails to many users
Secretly mining cryptocurrency on a victim's device
29.x: A Denial of Service attack floods a server with fake traffic so real users are blocked; a DDoS uses many machines such as a botnet.

29.s: What is e-mail bombing?
o: Sending the same e-mail repeatedly to one address to overflow it
Sending an e-mail that appears to come from another source
Sending deceptive e-mails to steal passwords
Hiding malware inside an e-mail attachment
29.x: E-mail bombing floods one inbox by sending the same message again and again; spoofing fakes the sender.

29.s: What is SQL injection?
o: Sending the same e-mail repeatedly to one address
Entering malicious database code through a website's input fields
Phishing carried out by voice calls
Secretly intercepting communication between two parties
29.x: SQL injection sends malicious database code through a website's input fields.

29.s: Which attack enters malicious database code through the input fields of a website?
29.x: SQL injection uses website input fields to send malicious database code.

29.s: In the context of computer security, crackers are also known as
29.x: Crackers are malicious (black-hat) hackers; white hats are ethical hackers and script kiddies are unskilled users of ready tools.

29.s: A person who gains illegal access to a computer system is known as
29.src: Grama Ward Sachivalayam Category-III Village Fisheries Assis
29.x: A hacker is a person who gains illegal (unauthorised) access to a computer system; a cracker is a malicious hacker and 'phracker' a phone hacker.

29.s: One who gains unauthorized access, destroys vital data, denies legitimate user's service or causes problems for their targets is called
29.x: A cracker (black-hat hacker) gains unauthorised access, destroys data or denies service; a white-hat hacker is ethical.

29.s: Cybercrime is :
29.x: Hacking, stalking and denial-of-service attacks are all cyber crimes.

29.s: Which of the following is not a cybercrime?
29.x: Online chatting is not a cybercrime; phishing, cyber stalking and identity theft are.

29.s: What is Digital arrest?
o: Arrest made by police when the accused is in foreign countries
Arrest made by police when the accused cannot be arrested physically
Arrest made by police when the accused is granted anticipatory bail by courts
Term used by cyber criminals to scare victims
29.x: 'Digital arrest' is a scam term: criminals pose as police, CBI or ED on video calls to frighten and extort victims; Indian law has no such arrest.

29.s: Deviant acts committed through information technology are referred to as
29.src: Grama Ward Sachivalayam Ward Planning & Development Secretar
29.x: Deviant acts committed through information technology are cyber crimes.

29.s: Which of the following is a characteristic of the dark web?
o: It is a secure government-only network used exclusively for defence communication.
It is a hidden part of the internet, reachable through tools such as Tor, and may host illicit marketplaces and data dumps.
It is the publicly indexed portion of the internet accessible through ordinary search engines.
It is a type of antivirus database maintained by CERT-In.
29.x: The dark web is a hidden part of the internet commonly accessed through tools such as Tor. It may contain illicit marketplaces, hacking tools and data dumps.
29.tq: Separate a hidden network from the ordinary publicly indexed web.
xs: The dark web is **a hidden part of the internet, reachable through tools such as Tor**, hosting **illicit marketplaces and data dumps** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It also hosts **hacking tools**; it is not the indexed web.
xa: Stolen data — **personal, medical, IP** — is sold on the dark web.
CERT-In is a **CVE Numbering Authority**, not a dark-web database.

29.s: In digital-arrest cases, the Supreme Court directed SOPs to be framed by the Centre, States, RBI and which other authority?
29.x: The directions called for SOPs by the Centre, States, RBI and telecom authorities, use of zero FIRs and restoration of victims' money.
xa: NCRP digital-arrest complaints fell from **1,23,672 (2024)** to **58,249 (2025)**.
Current relevance mentions **time-bound refunds**.

29.s: Identity theft is punishable under which section of the IT Act, 2000?
29.x: Identity theft falls under Section 66C; Sections 66E/67A apply to sextortion.
xa: **Sec. 43A** is compensation for failure to protect **sensitive personal data**.
**Digital arrest:** fake police/CBI officials keep a victim on video call to **extort money**.
**SIM swap** lets fraudsters intercept **OTPs**.

29.s: What does cyber slavery refer to?
o: Using a VPN to conceal a victim's browsing history
Trafficking people and forcing them to conduct cyber fraud
Stealing a person's identity to obtain a duplicate SIM
Selling stolen data through encrypted e-mail
29.x: Cyber slavery involves trafficking victims and coercing them to run cyber-fraud schemes, often from scam centres.
xa: **Telangana** police registered one of India's first such cases (per **INTERPOL**; APPSC-G2 **2023** PYQ).
Scam centres linked to **Myanmar and Laos** (MEA **2025**).

29.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about cyber slavery and scam centres?
o: Telangana Police registered one of India's first such cases.
FIU-India flagged Rs 8,000 crore in cross-border laundering linked to it.
Victims were trafficked and forced to commit cyber fraud.
Scam centres linked to it have been traced to Myanmar and Laos.
29.x: FIU-India flagged Rs 800 crore, not Rs 8,000 crore, in cross-border laundering linked to the issue.

29.s: Sextortion, blackmail using intimate images, is dealt with under which IT Act sections?

29.x: The dark web is reached via Tor and sextortion is blackmail with intimate images; digital arrest is a scam, not a real police power.

29.s: What is meant by crypto-jacking?

Stealing a cryptocurrency exchange's physical building
Scanning a QR code to receive cryptocurrency
Using a victim's device secretly to mine cryptocurrency

29.s: In a SIM swap fraud, why does the fraudster obtain a duplicate SIM?

29.x: Crime-as-a-service syndicates rent out ransomware and fraud tools; crypto-jacking is secret mining on a victim's device.

29.s: Which among the following filters information coming over the internet to a network or a computer system?

29.s: Virtual Keyboards protect the computer against :

29.x: Confidentiality covers the procedures, policies and controls that protect data from illicit access or use; integrity guards against alteration, availability against denial.

29.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the CIA triad of information security?

Preventing doctors from accessing a hospital system compromises integrity
Exposure, alteration and denial of access together hit all three elements

29.s: AES is an example of which type of cryptography?

xa: **Digital signature** proves **origin and integrity**.

29.s: Which key of the sender is used to verify a digital signature?
29.x: A digital signature is made with the sender's private key and verified with the corresponding public key.

29.s: What is hashing?
o: One-way process producing a fixed-length digest
Method of sharing one secret key with all users
Process using only the sender's private key to sign
29.x: Hashing is one-way and produces a fixed-length digest; even a small input change alters the hash (e.g. SHA-256).

29.s: RSA is an example of which type of encryption?

29.x: SHA-256 is a hash function giving a one-way, fixed-length digest; AES and Blowfish are symmetric and RSA is asymmetric.

29.s: What is logging in with a password followed by an OTP or biometric proof known as?

29.s: A security team exposes a decoy computer to attract intruders and observe their methods. What is the decoy called?

29.s:

29.s: Which malware is a virtual keyboard mainly used to defeat?

**Antivirus** prevents and heals infections; a **honeypot** is a decoy for attackers.
xa: ⚠ **Firewall** = blocks unauthorised access; **Antivirus** = prevents and heals infections.
**VPN** = encrypted tunnel over a public network.
Cyber security scope: **firewalls, encryption, passwords**.

29.s: What is "phishing" in cybersecurity?

Data was copied without the knowledge of the owner
The owner was denied access to the data
The data was denied from backup and restore facility

29.s: In computer terminology, the full form of malware is

29.x: Malware is short for malicious software. Cyber-security topic.

29.x: Ransomware hit the servers of the AP and Telangana power utilities in 2019.

29.s: DRDO-led Exercise Cyber Suraksha is associated with which of the following?

Training bank customers in digital payments over 12 months

Training the armed forces in cyber preparedness over 12 days

30.s: Which act provided legal recognition for transactions carried out by means of electronic data interchange and other means of electronic communication, commonly referred to as 'electronic commerce'?

30.x: The IT Act 2000 introduced electronic record, digital signature and certifying authority – all of the above.

30.x: In Shreya Singhal (24 March 2015) the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A as violating free speech under Article 19(1)(a).

30.s: Where an offence is squarely covered by the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Act may override the corresponding provisions of which law?
30.x: The Information Technology Act operates as a special law and may override IPC provisions where the offence is squarely covered by it.
30.tq: Identify the general law displaced by a special law.
xs: As a **special Act**, the IT Act overrides **Indian Penal Code** provisions where the crime is squarely covered — so option **(4)** is correct.

xa: Framework: **adjudication** of cyber contraventions, security of sensitive personal data, **intermediary due diligence**.

30.s: The Information Technology Act, 2000 was amended in which year to make the framework technology-neutral by recognising the term “electronic signature”?
30.x: The 2008 amendment introduced a technology-neutral approach by using the broader term “electronic signature.”

xa: Secs. **4-5** legally recognise electronic records and signatures.
**CERT-In** got statutory backing under **Sec. 70B** (inserted 2008).

30.s: Who issues Digital Signature Certificates under the Public Key Infrastructure framework?
o: Certifying Authorities licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities

o: Creation of the National Cyber Coordination Centre
Setting up of the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre
Setting up of the Data Protection Board

30.s: Legal recognition of electronic signatures is provided by which section of the IT Act, 2000?

30.x: Section 79A empowers the Centre to notify Examiners of Electronic Evidence.

30.x: Section 4 recognises electronic records and Section 5 recognises electronic signatures.

30.s: Which section of the IT Act, 2000 gives 'safe harbour' to intermediaries?
