42.s: In the reduced or microgravity of Space, the astronauts ' faces become red and bloated due to the blood and cerebrospinal fluid shifting towards the head causing them to have round, puffy faces and thinner legs. This phenomenon is known as:
42.x: The Charlie Brown effect is the fluid shift in microgravity that gives astronauts a puffy face and thin legs; the other names are distractors.

42.s: Weightlessness is –
42.x:
Most books: zero gravity. Strictly: weightlessness is free fall — gravity still acts (about 90% of surface g at ISS height); only the normal (support) force is zero (app notes 5:42 sub 6).
Key 'zero gravity', as books give: weightlessness is the state of no apparent weight, felt in free fall when nothing supports the body.

42.s: If the gravitational force of the Earth suddenly disappears, which are of the following will be the correct consequence?
o: The weight of an object will become zero but the mass
The mass of the object will become zero but the weight
Both the mass and the weight of the object will become
The mass of the object will increase
42.x: Weight = mass x g, so without gravity weight becomes zero but mass, the amount of matter, stays the same.

42.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about microgravity and space medicine?
o: Space medicine is studied only through actual spaceflight, not ground analogues.
Radiation exposure increases the risk of cancer and cataracts.
Daily resistance and treadmill exercise are used as countermeasures.
Diet and medication are part of the countermeasure strategy.
42.x: Space medicine is also studied through ground analogues such as Leh and HOPE.
xa: **Muscle atrophy** weakens postural muscles; Ax-4 tested **muscle regeneration**.
Bone loss: **1-1.5%** per month without load.
**Fluid shift**: "puffy face, bird legs".

42.s: What does Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) mainly cause?
o: Space motion sickness in the first days
Optic disc swelling and vision changes
42.x: SANS causes optic disc swelling and vision changes; space motion sickness is Space Adaptation Syndrome.
xa: SANS = **Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome**.
**Radiation exposure** raises **cancer and cataract** risk.
Bone loss: **1-1.5%** per month without load.

42.s: Which of the following weightlessness situations is INCORRECTLY explained?
o: Centre of Earth – Gravitational pull becomes negligible with distance
Freely falling lift – The floor no longer pushes up, so normal force is zero
Orbiting satellite – Satellite and astronaut accelerate towards Earth with the same g
Deep space far from all masses – Gravitational pull becomes negligible with distance
42.x: At the Earth's centre true g is zero because the pulls of the surrounding mass cancel; negligible pull with distance is the deep-space case.
n: At the centre of Earth, g equals zero. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
In free fall, the normal force becomes zero. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
An orbiting satellite and its astronaut both accelerate towards Earth with the same g. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
Apparent weight N is zero when effective gravity is zero. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
xa: Apparent weight **N** is zero when **effective gravity** is zero.
Microgravity experiments study **fluid behaviour**, **crystal growth** and **human physiology**.
Astronauts in space stations are in **continuous free fall**.

42.s: To what does the expression "puffy face, bird legs" in relation to astronauts refer?
o: Fluid shifting towards the head in microgravity
Loss of bone mass in the legs
42.x: Microgravity causes body fluids to shift towards the head, producing a puffy face and comparatively thinner-looking legs.
42.tq: Distinguish fluid redistribution from bone loss and muscle atrophy.
xs: "**Puffy face, bird legs**" describes **fluid shift** — fluids move towards the **head** — option **(3)**.
Bone loss is **osteopenia**; radiation raises **cancer and cataract** risk — neither is this effect.
xa: **Space Adaptation Syndrome** = space motion sickness in the first days.
**SANS** = optic disc swelling, vision changes.
Space medicine is studied on the **ISS** and in ground analogues (**Leh**, **HOPE**).

42.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about astronauts in an orbiting satellite?
o: The satellite and the astronaut accelerate towards Earth with the same g
The mass of the astronaut becomes zero
There is no normal force on the astronaut
42.x: The satellite and astronaut fall together with the same g, so the normal force is zero and the astronaut feels weightless; the astronaut's mass stays the same.
n: Apparent weight is zero inside an orbiting satellite. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]
An orbiting satellite and its astronaut both accelerate towards Earth with the same g. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 96-98]

42.s: What is the space motion sickness experienced by astronauts called?
42.x: Space Adaptation Syndrome is space motion sickness; SANS causes optic disc swelling.

42.s: In microgravity, astronauts lose about how much bone mass a month?
42.x: Bone loss in space is about 1–1.5% of bone mass a month.

42.s: What is the weight of a body on the Moon compared with its weight on Earth?
42.x: Weight on the Moon is about 1/6 of the weight on Earth.

⚠ The **Moon Agreement 1979** is the only one India **signed but not ratified**.

46.s: Which space treaty has India signed but not ratified?
46.x: The Moon Agreement is the only one India has signed but not ratified.
xa: **Outer Space Treaty 1967**: **no national sovereignty**; India ratified it in **1982**.

The Moon Agreement treats the Moon as **common heritage of mankind**.

46.s: What is the nature of a launching State's liability under the Liability Convention, 1972, for damage caused by its space object?
o: Absolute for damage on the Earth's surface and fault-based for damage in outer space
Fault-based for damage on the Earth's surface and absolute for damage in outer space
Absolute in all cases, whether the damage is on Earth or in outer space
Limited to damage caused by private operators only
46.x: The Liability Convention (1972), to which India is a party, makes the launching State absolutely liable for damage on the Earth's surface and liable only for fault for damage caused in outer space. Option B reverses the two rules. Option C ignores the fault standard in space. Option D is wrong because liability rests on the launching State, including for private activity.
46.tq: Liability Convention: Earth = absolute; space = fault.
xs: **Absolute** liability for damage **on Earth**, **fault** liability **in space** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) reverses the two rules; option (3) ignores the fault rule in space.
Liability lies on the **launching State** (OST **Art. VI** covers private actors too).
xa: India is a **party** to the Liability Convention.
OST **Art. VII** also covers liability.
India has **no Space Activities Act** for liability.

46.s: Which Article of the Outer Space Treaty deals with liability?
46.x: Article VII deals with liability; Article VI is national responsibility and Article IX due regard.

48.x: Agni-I is a single-stage solid-fuel missile with a range of about 700–800 km and is approximately 15 metres long.

xs: **Agni-I** is a **single-stage solid-fuel** missile of about **700-800 km** range — option **(2)**.
It is about **15 m** long, with accurate navigation.
**2,000-3,000 km** is **Agni-II** (two-stage solid); **150 km** liquid is **Prithvi-I**; **5,000 km** three-stage is **Agni-V**.
xa: Agni-I is **nuclear-capable**, fired by the Army from **road-mobile TEL** trucks.
Agni-I test: **ITR Balasore**, **22 May 2026**.
⚠ Some notes give Agni-I as **~700-900 km** (SRBM/MRBM).

48.s: How many stages does Agni-V, a solid-fuel, canister-launched missile, have?
48.x: Agni-V is a three-stage solid-fuel, canister-launched missile with a stated range of 5,000 km or more; MIRV has been tested with it.
xa: Agni-V is **fully indigenous** — ⚠ "not exclusively indigenous" is the wrong statement (UPPSC **2015**).
**Dr Tessy Thomas** played a key role in Agni-V.
⚠ Formally **IRBM** class: the ICBM threshold is **5,500 km**.

48.s: Which of the following pairs about the Agni series is correctly matched?
48.x: Agni-II is a two-stage solid-fuel missile (2,000–3,500 km). Agni-IV is two-stage and road-mobile (about 4,000 km), Agni-III has about 3,500 km range, and the three-stage canisterised missile is Agni-V.

48.s: From which platform was Agni-Prime test-fired on 24 September 2025?
48.x: Agni-Prime, a canisterised 1,000–2,000 km missile, was fired from a rail-based mobile launcher.
xa: Agni series operator: **Strategic Forces Command**.
**Agni-4** user trial: **ITR Chandipur, 6 Aug 2026**.
An advanced Agni with **MIRV** was tested on **8 May 2026**.

48.s: Mission Divyastra (2024) tested MIRV technology on which missile?
48.x: Mission Divyastra, conducted in 2024, flight-tested Agni-V with Multiple Independently targetable Re-entry Vehicles (MIRVs).
xa: Advanced Agni with a **MIRV** was tested on **8 May 2026**.
Agni-V: **three-stage solid**, **canister-launched**, **5,000+ km**.
All 2026 Agni tests were under the **Strategic Forces Command**.

48.s: What is the formal ICBM range threshold that places Agni-V's 5,000 km range in the IRBM class?
48.x: The ICBM threshold cited is 5,500 km, so Agni-V is formally an IRBM, though some sources call it an ICBM.
xa: **Agni-VI** is the **proposed longer-range ICBM**.
Agni-V is **three-stage solid** and **canister-launched**.
Advanced Agni with a **MIRV** was tested on **8 May 2026**.

48.s: Which Agni variant is a two-stage, road-mobile missile with a range of about 4,000 km?
48.x: Agni-IV is two-stage and road-mobile with about 4,000 km range; Agni-V is three-stage with 5,000+ km.

48.s: What is PINAKA?
48.src: APPSC Extension Officer Grade-I Common Paper General Studies
48.x: Pinaka is DRDO's multi-barrel rocket launcher (ARDE, Pune) – an artillery rocket system, not a missile.

48.s:
The major success of the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) has been in the missile programme. So far it has successfully test-fired the following missiles for the defence forces.

A. Prithvi: Surface to surface missile

B. Trishul: Surface to Air missile

C. Akash: Surface to Air missile

D. Nag: Anti-tank guided missile

E. Agni: Sea launched cruise missile
Select the correct answer from the codes given below:
o: A, B, C and D only
48.x: Prithvi is surface-to-surface, Trishul and Akash are surface-to-air and Nag is an anti-tank guided missile, so A-D are correct. Agni is a land-based surface-to-surface ballistic missile, not a sea-launched cruise missile, so E is wrong.

48.s: Find the incorrect pair
48.x: Nag is a third-generation fire-and-forget anti-tank missile, not a surface-to-air missile, so that pair is incorrect. Prithvi and Agni are surface-to-surface and Trishul is surface-to-air.

48.s: Which one of the following is a Submarine-Launched Ballistic Missile (SLBM)?
48.x: K-4 is a submarine-launched ballistic missile (~3,500 km) of the K-series for the Arihant-class submarines. Agni-4 and Prithvi are land-based and Akash is a SAM.

48.s: India’s short-range missile is –
48.x:
Official key / most books: Nag (shortest range). Strictly: Prithvi is the missile formally classed as a short-range ballistic missile (SRBM) (PMF S&T Part 6 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-06.txt) p.62).
Among the options Nag has the shortest range (500 m – 4 km), so most keys give Nag. Prithvi (150-350 km) is formally India's short-range ballistic missile, Agni is long-range and Arjun is a tank.

48.s: India’s surface to air missile is –
48.x: Trishul is a short-range, low-level surface-to-air missile of the IGMDP. Agni and Prithvi are surface-to-surface and Nag is anti-tank.

48.s: Which of the following is India's surface to surface defence missile –
48.x: Prithvi is India's surface-to-surface short-range ballistic missile. Trishul and Akash are surface-to-air and Nag is anti-tank.

48.s: Which of the following Indian missile is surface to surface missile?
48.x: Prithvi is a surface-to-surface SRBM. Trishul and Akash are surface-to-air missiles, and Nag is an anti-tank missile.

48.s: Which of these missiles is not part of the Integrated Guided Missile Programme of India?
48.x: BrahMos is an India-Russia supersonic cruise missile (BrahMos Aerospace), not part of the IGMDP. Akash, Prithvi and Agni are IGMDP missiles.

48.s: Which of the following is not a missile?
48.x: Pinaka is a multi-barrel rocket launcher, not a missile. Agni, Akash and Nag are all IGMDP missiles.

48.s: What is the range of Prithvi, a liquid-fuelled surface-to-surface short-range ballistic missile?
48.x: Prithvi is a surface-to-surface SRBM with a range of 150–350 km and uses liquid fuel.
xa: ⚠ **Prithvi = liquid**; **Agni = solid**.
**Prithvi-I** (Army) **150 km**; **Prithvi-II** (Air Force) **350 km**.
**Dhanush** = naval, **ship-launched** version of Prithvi.
The name Prithvi means **Earth**.

48.s: At about what speed does Akash, a medium-range surface-to-air missile, travel?
48.x: Akash is a medium-range SAM with a range of about 25-30 km, a speed of about Mach 2.5 and an altitude capability of 18 km.
xa: Base Akash: launch weight **720 kg**.
**Akash Prime**: indigenous **active RF seeker**; **Akash-NG**: about **70 km**, canister-launched.
⚠ **Akashteer** (BEL + Army) is an air-defence **control** system, NOT a missile.

48.s: Which missile has a range of about 25–30 km?
48.x: Akash, a medium-range SAM, has a range of about 25–30 km. Trishul reaches about 9 km, Nag 500 m to 4 km (land version), and Agni about 700 km to over 5,000 km.

48.s: Which of the following missile names is NOT correctly matched with its meaning?
48.x: Trishul means Trident; it is Agni that means Fire.

48.s:
Consider the following statements about Trishul:
1. It is a short-range, low-level quick-reaction surface-to-air missile.
2. Its range is about 9 km.
3. It was inducted into the Army.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
48.x: Trishul is a short-range quick-reaction SAM of about 9 km range, but it was never inducted and was shut in 2008.

48.s: What is DRDO's Lakshya?
48.x: Lakshya is a target drone; Pinaka is a rocket launcher, Tejas an aircraft and Nishant a UAV.
xa: **Arjun** = tank; **Rustom** = UAV; **NAMICA** = Nag carrier vehicle.
⚠ **BrahMos** was **not part of IGMDP**.

48.s: With which country did India jointly develop BrahMos, which was not a missile of the IGMDP?
48.x: BrahMos was developed jointly by India and Russia; it was not part of the IGMDP.

48.s:
Identify the statements that are correct with regard to the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP) initiated by DRDO in 1983

A. The basic objective of the programme is to attain self-sufficiency in the field of missile technology

B. To develop a family of strategic and tactical guided missiles

C. Agni, Akash and Trishul are among the missiles developed under the programme

D. To be the first country in the world to have international market for missiles
48.x: IGMDP (1983) aimed at self-sufficiency in missile technology through a family of strategic and tactical guided missiles, and produced Agni, Akash and Trishul (with Prithvi and Nag). Building an international missile market was never an objective, so D is wrong.

48.s: Which of the following missiles were developed by Integrated Guided Missile Development programme (IGMDP)
48.x: The five IGMDP missiles are Prithvi, Agni, Trishul, Akash and Nag. Astra, Dhanush, Shaurya, Nirbhay, Sagarika, Helina, Prahaar and Barak-8 came later or outside it.

48.s: Under the IGMDP, which missile was developed during the 1992–2008 phase?
48.x: Prithvi and Trishul were developed in 1984–89, Nag and Akash in 1989–92, and Agni in 1992–2008.
xa: IGMDP was **launched in 1983** under **Dr APJ Abdul Kalam**.
After **2008**, later missiles were developed as **separate projects**.
⚠ **Trishul**, from the first phase, was the IGMDP missile **never inducted**.

48.s: Which was the nodal laboratory of the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP)?
48.x: DRDL, Hyderabad was the nodal lab, working with RCI and ASL; IGMDP was launched in 1983 under Kalam.
xa: Phases: **1984-89** Prithvi + Trishul; **1989-92** Nag + Akash; **1992-2008** Agni.
Spin-offs: **ring laser gyros**, composites, radomes.
⚠ **BrahMos** was **not part of IGMDP**.

48.s: Under the Ministry of Defence approval, to whom is the technology of conventional missiles such as Nag transferred?
48.x: Conventional missiles, including Nag, go to private industry, while Agni remains in state production.
xa: **Nag**: **4-7 km**, **fire-and-forget**, **IIR** seeker.
**Agni** is operated by the **Strategic Forces Command**.
Agni is built by **DRDO** — ⚠ not ISRO.

48.s: Which one of the following is NOT an identified spin-off of the IGMDP?
48.x: Long-range tracking systems, composites, ring laser gyros and radomes were identified as IGMDP spin-offs. A satellite-based navigation constellation is not included in this list.
48.tq: Find the item outside the stated group of technological spin-offs.
xs: A **satellite-based navigation constellation** is not listed among IGMDP spin-offs — option **(1)**.
The listed spin-offs are the **long-range tracking system**, **composites**, **ring laser gyros** and **radomes**.
xa: **Agni-IV** uses a **ring-laser-gyro INS** with **RINS + MINGS** navigation.
IGMDP was **launched in 1983** and **completed in 2008**.
Nodal lab: **DRDL Hyderabad**.

48.s: Why is the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme regarded as significant?
o: Ended all missile development in India after the completion of Prithvi.
Turned India from a missile importer into a missile-exporting power and formed a base for later Agni-V MIRV, BMD and BrahMos-era programmes.
Restricted India to importing surface-to-air missiles from foreign suppliers.
Was created exclusively for developing civilian launch vehicles.
48.x: The IGMDP transformed India from a missile importer into a missile-exporting power and provided the foundation for Agni-V MIRV, ballistic missile defence and BrahMos-era programmes.
48.tq: Select the option that captures both the strategic transformation and the later technological base.
xs: IGMDP turned India from a **missile importer** into a **missile-exporting power**, and laid the base for **Agni-V MIRV, BMD and BrahMos-era programmes** — option **(2)**.
Missile work did not end: after **2008**, later missiles came as **separate projects**.
xa: Launched in **1983** under **Dr APJ Abdul Kalam**, after the **1962, 1965, 1971** wars.
**Mission Divyastra (2024)**: Agni-V with **MIRV**.
Spin-offs: **long-range tracking system**, **composites**, **ring laser gyros**, **radomes**.

48.s: In which year was the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (IGMDP) officially completed?
48.x: IGMDP ran from 1983 and was officially completed in 2008; later missiles became separate projects.

48.s: In which year was the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme launched?
48.x: IGMDP was launched in 1983 under Dr APJ Abdul Kalam and was officially completed in 2008.

48.s: Which missiles were developed in the first phase (1984-89) of the IGMDP?
48.x: Prithvi and Trishul came in the first phase (1984-89); Nag and Akash in 1989-92; Agni matured by 2008.

48.s: Which of the following is a ' Fire and Forget ' antitank missile?
48.x: Nag is a third-generation fire-and-forget ATGM with an imaging infrared seeker, so it guides itself after launch. Agni and Prithvi are ballistic missiles, and BrahMos is a cruise missile, not an anti-tank weapon.

48.s: On December 11 India tested indigenously designed SANT missile at
48.x: DRDO and the IAF flight-tested the helicopter-launched SANT (stand-off anti-tank) missile from the Pokhran ranges, Rajasthan, on 11 December 2021. Balasore/Chandipur and Thiruvananthapuram were not the site.

48.s: Which is a "Fire and forget" anti-tank missile?
48.src: APPSC AE (Environmental) Mains General Studies & Mental Abil
48.x: Nag is the third-generation fire-and-forget anti-tank missile. Akash is a SAM, Astra an air-to-air missile and Prahar a tactical surface-to-surface missile.

48.s: In 2019 the Defence Research and Development Organization (DRDO) successfully flight tested an indigenously developed low weight, fire and forget, man portable anti tank guided missile from a firing range at
48.src: Grama Ward Sachivalayam Category-III Village Fisheries Assis
48.x: In 2019 DRDO flight-tested the man-portable fire-and-forget anti-tank guided missile (MPATGM) at the Kurnool ranges in Andhra Pradesh. Sriharikota is ISRO's launch site.

48.s: 'Nag' is a/an
48.x: Nag is a third-generation fire-and-forget anti-tank missile, not a multi-rocket system (Pinaka) or a surface-to-air / surface-to-surface missile.

48.s: India's Anti tank missile is-
48.x: Nag is India's fire-and-forget anti-tank missile (range 500 m – 4 km). Agni is a ballistic missile, Akash a SAM and Vajra a self-propelled gun.

48.s: HELINA is the helicopter-launched version of which missile?
48.x: HELINA is the helicopter-launched Nag, a fire-and-forget anti-tank missile.
xa: Nag: **IIR** seeker and an **8 kg HEAT tandem warhead**.
**NAMIS** (Nag Mk-2) is also fire-and-forget — the tracked "**tank killer**".
⚠ "Which is a fire-and-forget anti-tank missile?" → **Nag** (not Prithvi, Akash or Trishul).

48.s: What is meant by the term 'fire-and-forget' in missile technology?
o: The missile is incapable of changing its course after launch.
The missile can guide itself after launch, allowing the operator to take cover.
The missile is fired only after the target has been destroyed by another weapon.
The missile must remain continuously controlled by the operator until impact.
48.x: A fire-and-forget missile guides itself after launch, enabling the operator to seek cover or perform another task.
48.tq: Translate the technical term into its operational consequence.
xs: **Fire-and-forget**: the missile **guides itself after launch**, so the operator can **take cover** — option **(2)**.
Examples: **Nag**, **HELINA**, **MPATGM**.
xa: **Top attack**: missile climbs, then dives onto the tank's thin **top armour**.
**Nag** has both **top-attack** and **direct-attack** modes.
Nag is a **third-generation** fire-and-forget ATGM (APPSC-G1 **2018** key).

48.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
48.x: Nag uses an Imaging Infra-Red seeker, whereas Akash Prime uses an active RF seeker and SANT uses Lock-On After Launch. Therefore, Nag with an active RF seeker is not correctly matched.
48.tq: Find the one swapped seeker associated with a different missile.
xs: **Nag — active RF seeker** is wrongly matched — option **(4)**.
Nag uses an **Imaging Infra-Red (IIR)** seeker; the **active RF seeker** belongs to **Akash Prime**.
**SANT** uses **Lock-On After Launch** — correctly matched.
xa: **Akash Prime** = upgraded **Akash Mk-I**, first tested **27 Sep 2021**.
**Akash Mk-I** uses command guidance with the **Rajendra radar**.
Other guidance types: **laser**, **GPS**, **electro-optical**.

48.s: What is Nag Mk-2, the tracked fire-and-forget 'tank killer' approved for Army procurement, called?
48.x: NAMIS is the tracked Nag Mk-2; Dhruvastra is the IAF's helicopter-launched Nag, HELINA the Army Aviation version and SANT an air-launched stand-off ATGM.
xa: **NAMICA** = tracked amphibious **Nag Missile Carrier**, carries up to **six** missiles.
**HELINA** (about **7 km**) is for **Army Aviation**.
**SANT** range: **15-20 km**.

48.s: For which service is HELINA, the helicopter-launched variant of the Nag missile, meant?
48.x: HELINA is the helicopter-launched Nag variant for Army Aviation, whereas Dhruvastra is intended for the Indian Air Force.
xa: ⚠ Remember: **HELINA** = Army Aviation; **Dhruvastra** = IAF.
HELINA is a **fire-and-forget** missile, like Nag and MPATGM.
**SANT** is the **air-launched stand-off** ATGM (**15-20 km**).

48.s: Each Nag Missile Carrier (NAMICA) can carry up to how many missiles?
48.x: Each NAMICA, a tracked amphibious vehicle, can carry up to six Nag missiles.
xa: Nag is a **third-generation fire-and-forget ATGM** (APPSC-G1 **2018** key), range **4-7 km**.
Its **Imaging Infra-Red (IIR)** seeker gives **night-strike** capability.
**Nag Mk-2 / NAMIS** — tracked "**tank killer**", approved for Army procurement (**2026**).
⚠ NAMICA is a **carrier vehicle**, not a missile.

48.s: What does an anti-tank missile generally do in the top-attack mode?
o: Approaches at ground level and hits the side armour
Climbs and then dives onto the tank's thinner top armour
Strikes the thick frontal armour head-on
Hits the tracks to immobilise the tank
48.x: In top attack, the missile climbs and then dives onto the tank's thinner top armour; Nag has both top-attack and direct-attack modes.
xa: Nag's **IIR** seeker gives **night-strike** capability.
**SANT** uses a **Lock-On After Launch** seeker.
Not missiles: **Arjun** (tank), **Pinaka** (rocket launcher), **NAMICA** (Nag carrier).

48.s: For which service is Dhruvastra, the helicopter-launched Nag variant, meant?
48.x: HELINA is the Army Aviation version, while Dhruvastra is the IAF version.

48.s: Which guidance mode does SANT, the air-launched stand-off anti-tank missile, use?
48.x: SANT (15–20 km) uses Lock-On After Launch (LOAL).

48.s: What is the range of the Nag-family MPATGM, a man-portable anti-tank missile?
48.x: MPATGM reaches about 2.5 km; NAMIS reaches 7–10 km and SANT 15–20 km.

48.s: The Nag anti-tank missile uses which type of seeker?
48.x: Nag uses an IIR seeker; Akash Prime uses an active RF seeker.

48.s: Which of the following missiles developed by India can be used from ship to ship?
48.x:
Official key / most books: Dhanush. Strictly: BrahMos is also ship-to-ship capable (ship-launched anti-ship cruise missile, PMF S&T Part 6 (src/science-tech/pmf-science-tech-06.txt) p.57 table "Ship-Launched Missile: BrahMos, Dhanush").
Dhanush, the naval version of Prithvi, is fired from ships (ship-to-ship and ship-to-shore). Agni and Akash are land-based. BrahMos also has a ship-launched anti-ship version, but it is an India-Russia cruise missile, not the expected answer.

48.s: Out of the following, Dhanush is
o: A mini nuclear reactor using Thorium fuel
A long range ballistic missile to be used by Army
A short range ballistic missile to be used by Navy
A satellite to study the interstellar matter
48.src: APPSC Royalty Inspector, Agriculture Officer, Town Planning
48.x: Dhanush is the naval, ship-launched version of Prithvi – a short-range ballistic missile for the Navy, not an Army long-range missile, a reactor or a satellite.

48.s:
Consider the following statements :

A. In November, 2006, DRDO successfully conducted the interception test using Prithvi II missile.

B. Prithvi-II is a surface-to-surface missile and can be deployed to guard the metros against air attacks.
Which of the statements given above is / are correct?
48.x: On 27 November 2006 DRDO's PAD interceptor (a modified Prithvi) destroyed a Prithvi-II target – the interception test of statement A. Prithvi-II is an offensive surface-to-surface missile, not a weapon to guard metros against air attack, so B is wrong.

48.s: Name the missile tested by Indian scientists and defence personnel on 27.1.96 at Chandipur :
48.x: Prithvi-II was first test-fired on 27 January 1996 from Chandipur. Prithvi-I was tested in 1988, Akash is a SAM and PSLV-D2 a launch vehicle.

48.s:
Consider the following statements about Prithvi-II Missile.

I. It is a nuclear-capable Ballistic missile.

II. It has a maximum range of 100 km.

III. It is India’s first native made ballistic missile.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
48.x: Prithvi-II is nuclear-capable, so I is correct. Its range is 350 km, not 100 km, and Prithvi-I rather than Prithvi-II was India's first indigenous ballistic missile, so II and III are wrong.

48.s:
Consider the following statements.

I. The DRDO developed two variants of Prithvi missile.

II. Prithvi II is equipped with features of maneuverability to deceive the enemy.

III. Induction of Prithvi missile enhances the capability of the Indian Army to attack multiple targets simultaneously.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
48.x: Prithvi-II has a manoeuvring trajectory to evade interception, so II is correct. Prithvi has three variants (I, II and III/Dhanush), not two, so I is wrong; per the printed key, III is also not accepted.

48.s: Which was the first missile developed under the IGMDP?
48.x: Prithvi was the first IGMDP missile; Prithvi-I serves the Army and Prithvi-II the Air Force.
xa: **Prithvi-III / Dhanush** serves the **Navy** (ship-launched).
Prithvi-II was **first tested in 1996** and **inducted in 2003**.
Prithvi-II and Agni-I were **test-fired together** (**Jul 2025**).

48.s: Which type of fuel do Prithvi-I and Prithvi-II use?
48.x: Prithvi-I and Prithvi-II use liquid fuel, whereas Agni-I uses solid fuel.
xa: Prithvi-II and Agni-I were test-fired together in **Jul 2025**.
**Agni-I**: single-stage solid, about **700-800 km**, about **15 m** long.
An **Agni-1** test was held at **ITR Balasore** on **22 May 2026**.

48.s: In which year was Prithvi-II, first tested in 1996, inducted?
48.x: Prithvi-II was inducted in 2003; the naval version is Dhanush.
xa: Prithvi-II: **350 km**, payload **500-1,000 kg**, **nuclear-capable SRBM**.
Dhanush means **Bow**.
**PAD / Pradyumna** is the Prithvi-based exo-atmospheric interceptor.

48.s: Which service operates Dhanush, the ship-launched version of the Prithvi missile?
48.x: Dhanush (Prithvi-III) is the Navy's ship-launched Prithvi; Prithvi-I is the Army's 150 km version.

48.s: Which service operates Prithvi-II, the variant with a range of about 350 km?
48.x: Prithvi-II is the Air Force version; Prithvi-I is the Army's and Dhanush the Navy's.

48.s: What is PAD (Pradyumna) in India's missile programme?
48.x: PAD (Pradyumna) is an exo-atmospheric interceptor working at 50-80 km altitude.

48.s: Which service operates the Prithvi-I missile?
48.x: Prithvi-I (150 km) is the Army version; Prithvi-II is for the Air Force and Dhanush for the Navy.

48.s: Missile Akash was developed by
48.x: Akash was developed by DRDO under the IGMDP; DRDL, Hyderabad was its lead DRDO laboratory, so DRDO (the organisation) is the best answer. ISRO and BHEL did not develop it.

48.s: From which of the following place the indigenously developed Quick Reaction Surface-to-Air Missile (QRSAM) was test fired successfully in July 2017?
48.src: APPSC Group-III Panchayat Secretary Mains Paper-I General St
48.x: QRSAM, the indigenous quick-reaction SAM, was test-fired from the Integrated Test Range at Chandipur, Odisha, in 2017. Sriharikota is ISRO's launch port and Kalpakkam a nuclear site.

48.s: On 27 September 2021, DRDO tested a new version of the Akash Missile equipped with an active Radio Frequency (RF) seeker for improved accuracy. What is the name of this new version of Akash missile?
48.x: Akash Prime is the Akash version with an indigenous active RF seeker, first tested on 27 September 2021. Akash Next, Apex and Blaze are not Akash variants (the next-generation one is Akash-NG).

48.s: Which missile programme has been shelved by the DRDO?
48.x: DRDO shelved the Trishul programme, officially shutting it down on 27 February 2008, after delays and failures to meet requirements. Nag and Agni continued.

48.s: Which one of the following statements about Trishul is NOT correct?
o: Its commonly cited range is about 9 km.
It was inducted into regular service after successful development.
It is a short-range, low-level surface-to-air missile.
It uses solid fuel with thrust vector control.
48.x: Trishul was never inducted into regular service and the programme was closed in 2008. It is a short-range low-level SAM using solid fuel with thrust vector control.
48.tq: Find the wrong service-status statement rather than the missile’s technical features.
xs: Statement (2) is NOT correct: **Trishul** was **never inducted** and was **closed in 2008** — option **(2)**.
The other statements are correct: range about **9 km**, a **short-range, low-level SAM**, **solid fuel with thrust vector control**.
xa: Trishul was shut on **27 Feb 2008** after failing operational requirements, with **delays** and **cost overruns**.
Replacements: **Spyder** (IAF), **Barak-1** (Navy), **Akash** (Army).
Indigenous successor: **QRSAM** (Quick Reaction SAM).
Trishul means **Trident**.

48.s: Which services use the Akash surface-to-air missile?
48.x: Akash, a medium-range SAM of about 25-30 km, is used by the Army and the Indian Air Force.

48.s: In which year was the Trishul surface-to-air missile programme shut down?
48.x: Trishul was never inducted; the programme was shut on 27 February 2008.
xa: ⚠ Replacements: **Spyder** (IAF), **Barak-1** (Navy), **Akash** (Army).
Indigenous successor: **QRSAM**.
Trishul's range: ~**9 km** (some notes **12 km**).

48.s: On which date was Akash Prime, an upgraded Akash Mk-I with an indigenous active RF seeker, first tested?
48.x: Akash Prime was first tested on 27 September 2021.

51.s: The powerful explosive used under the name gun cotton is
51.x: Gun cotton is cellulose nitrate, made by treating cotton with nitric and sulphuric acids; cellulose acetate is not an explosive.

51.s: Which one of the following is another name of RDX?
51.x: RDX is also called cyclonite (and hexogen); chemically it is cyclotrimethylenetrinitramine.

51.s: Which one of the following is used as an explosive?
51.x: Nitroglycerine is a powerful explosive used in dynamite; phosphorus trichloride, mercuric oxide and graphite are not explosives.

51.s: What is the common characteristic of the chemical substances generally known as CL-20, HMX and LLM- 105, which are sometimes talked about in media?
o: These are alternatives to hydrofluorocarbon refrigerants
These are explosives in military weapons
These are high-energy fuels for cruise missiles
These are fuels for rocket propulsion
51.x: CL-20, HMX and LLM-105 are high explosives used in military weapons (CL-20 is the most powerful non-nuclear explosive; LLM-105 an insensitive high explosive). They are not refrigerants or fuels.

51.s: Which one of the following statement is correct?
51.x: RDX is an explosive. DDT is an insecticide, TNT an explosive (not an insecticide) and LSD a hallucinogen, not an antiviral.

51.s: 'Nobel oil' is the name of which one of the following explosives?
51.x: Trinitroglycerine (TNG), i.e. nitroglycerine, is known as Nobel's oil.

51.s: Which one of the following explosives does not contain nitroglycerine as an essential constituent ?
51.x: Amatol is TNT plus ammonium nitrate and contains no nitroglycerine, while cordite, blasting gelatine and dynamite all contain nitroglycerine.

51.s: Which one of the following is used as an explosive?
51.x: Nitroglycerine (glyceryl trinitrate) is an oily liquid explosive; phosphorus trichloride, mercuric oxide and graphite are not explosives.

51.s: Which one of the following is another name of RDX ?
51.x: RDX is also known as cyclonite; cyanohydrin, dextran and cyclohexane are unrelated compounds.

51.s: Which one of the following is not an explosive?
51.x: Nitrochloroform (chloropicrin) is a toxic fumigant, not an explosive, whereas TNG and TNT are explosives; potassium chlorate is a strong oxidiser used in explosive mixtures.

51.s: The explosive nitroglycerine is a
51.x: Nitroglycerine is glyceryl trinitrate, C3H5(ONO2)3, the nitrate ester of glycerol, so it is an ester, not a salt or a nitro-hydrocarbon.

51.s: Which of the following is not an explosive?
51.x: Nitrochloroform is not an explosive. Cyclotrimethylene trinitramine is RDX, and TNT and TNG are explosives too.

51.s: The chemical used in manufacturing of dynamite is
51.x: Dynamite is nitroglycerine absorbed in kieselguhr or sawdust, and nitroglycerine is glycerol trinitrate.

51.s: What is LLM-105?
51.x: LLM-105 is an insensitive high explosive with greater safety against accidental detonation.
xa: **CL-20**: most powerful non-nuclear explosive, by **HEMRL Pune**.
**HMX (octogen) / RDX**: powerful military explosives; ultra-fine **beta-HMX** from **TBRL**.
⚠ "Insensitive" = hard to set off by accident — the opposite of "most powerful".

51.s:
Consider the following statements about CL-20:
1. It is associated with HEMRL, Pune.
2. It is described as the most powerful non-nuclear explosive.
3. It is associated with TBRL, Chandigarh.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
51.x: CL-20 is associated with the High Energy Materials Research Laboratory (HEMRL), Pune, and is the most powerful non-nuclear explosive; it is not a TBRL product.

51.s: Which of the following is the formula of TNT?
51.x: TNT (trinitrotoluene) is C₆H₂(NO₂)₃CH₃, that is C₇H₅N₃O₆. C₃H₆N₆O₆ is RDX, C₆H₃N₃O₇ picric acid and C₃H₅(ONO₂)₃ nitroglycerine.
n: The formula of TNT is C₆H₂(NO₂)₃CH₃. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
The formula of TNT is C₇H₅N₃O₆. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
The formula of TNG is C₃H₅(ONO₂)₃. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
The formula of TNP is C₆H₃N₃O₇. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
The formula of RDX is C₃H₆N₆O₆. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
xs: **TNT** (**trinitrotoluene**) is **C₆H₂(NO₂)₃CH₃**, i.e. **C₇H₅N₃O₆** — option **(1)**.
**C₃H₆N₆O₆** is **RDX**; **C₆H₃N₃O₇** is **picric acid (TNP)**; **C₃H₅(ONO₂)₃** is **nitroglycerine (TNG)**.
xa: TNT is used in **military shells**, **bombs**, **grenades** and **underwater blasting**.
TNT is also an **intermediate** for **dyes** and **photographic chemicals**.
**CL-20** (HNIW) is **C₆H₆N₁₂O₁₂**.

51.s: By what name is trinitrophenol commonly known?
51.x: Trinitrophenol is picric acid; trinitroglycerine is Nobel's oil, RDX cyclonite and HMX octogen.
n: RDX is also called Cyclonite. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
HMX is also called Octogen. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Trinitroglycerine is also called Nobel oil. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Trinitrophenol is also called Picric acid. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
HMX is also called Octogen. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
TNG is also called Nobel oil. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Trinitrophenol is also called picric acid. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
xa: RDX is also **Hexogen** (**Germany**) and **T-4** (**Italy**).
HMX = **High Melting Explosive**, a related nitroamine.
**TBRL** makes ultra-fine **beta-HMX** and fine RDX.

51.s: By what other name is the explosive CL-20 known?
51.x: CL-20 is HNIW; HMX is High Melting Explosive.
n: TNG is nitroglycerine. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
CL-20 is also called HNIW. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Gun cotton is nitrated cellulose. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Trinitroglycerine is also called nitroglycerine. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
HMX is also called High Melting Explosive. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
xa: **CL-20** is among the most powerful non-nuclear explosives, synthesised by **HEMRL Pune**.
**LLM-105** is an **insensitive** high explosive.
Gun cotton is used in **rockets**, **propellants** and **celluloid**.

51.s: What is RDX chemically?
51.x: RDX is cyclotrimethylenetrinitramine; TNP is trinitrophenol and TNG is glyceryl trinitrate.
n: TNP is picric acid. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
The chemical name of TNG is trinitroglycerine. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
The chemical name of TNG is glyceryl trinitrate. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
The chemical name of TNP is trinitrophenol. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
The chemical name of RDX is cyclotrimethylenetrinitramine. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
The chemical name of HMX is High Melting Explosive. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
xa: TNP is **picric acid**; TNG is **Nobel oil**.
TNP uses: explosive, **laboratory reagent**, **dyes**, older **antiseptic** use.
HMX, CL-20, LLM-105 are used in **solid rocket** and **missile propellants**.

51.s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
51.x: RDX is (O₂NNCH₂)₃. TNG is C₃H₅(ONO₂)₃, TNP is (O₂N)₃C₆H₂OH and CL-20 is C₆H₆N₁₂O₁₂.
n: The formula of TNP is (O₂N)₃C₆H₂OH. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
The formula of RDX is (O₂NNCH₂)₃. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
The formula of CL-20 is C₆H₆N₁₂O₁₂. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
xa: TNP can also be written **C₆H₃N₃O₇**; RDX as **C₃H₆N₆O₆**.
**TNT** = **C₇H₅N₃O₆**.
CL-20 is also called **HNIW**.

51.s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Dynamite consists of nitroglycerine absorbed in sawdust or kieselguhr.
Blasting gelatin contains 91–93% nitroglycerine, 6–8% nitrocellulose and about 1% acid acceptor.
C-4 consists of HMX in a plastic matrix.
Amatol is composed of TNT and ammonium nitrate.
51.x: Option C is incorrect: C-4 plastic explosive is based on RDX, not HMX. The dynamite, blasting gelatin and amatol compositions are right.
51.tq: Recall RDX as the base of C-4.
n: Dynamite consists of nitroglycerine absorbed in kieselguhr or sawdust. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Amatol consists of TNT and ammonium nitrate. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
C-4 is a plastic explosive. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
RDX is the primary agent in C-4. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Dynamite contains nitroglycerine absorbed in sawdust. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Dynamite contains nitroglycerine absorbed in kieselguhr. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Amatol contains TNT and ammonium nitrate. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Blasting gelatin contains 91–93% nitroglycerine. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Blasting gelatin contains 6–8% nitrocellulose. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Blasting gelatin contains approximately 1% acid acceptor. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
C-4 contains RDX in a plastic matrix. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Blasting gelatin consists of nitroglycerine and nitrocellulose. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
xs: The incorrect statement is "**C-4 consists of HMX in a plastic matrix**" — option **(3)**: C-4 is **RDX** in a **plastic matrix**.
**Dynamite** = nitroglycerine absorbed in **kieselguhr** or **sawdust** — correct.
**Blasting gelatin** = **91–93%** nitroglycerine + **6–8%** nitrocellulose + **1%** acid acceptor; **Amatol** = **TNT + ammonium nitrate** — both correct.
xa: ⚠ **Amatol** contains **no nitroglycerine**.
**Cordite** is a **propellant** containing nitroglycerine.
**Gun cotton** = cotton or wood fibres treated with **HNO₃** and **H₂SO₄**.

51.s: Which explosive is also used in printing inks, leather finishing and celluloid?
51.x: Gun cotton is used in printing inks, leather finishing and celluloid; picric acid (TNP) is used in explosives and dyes.
n: Gun cotton is used in printing inks. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Gun cotton is used in leather finishing. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Gun cotton is used in celluloid. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
TNP is used as an explosive. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
TNP is used in dyes. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
xa: Gun cotton is also used in **rockets** and **propellants**.
TNP is also a **laboratory reagent**, with an older use as an **antiseptic**.
TNP = **picric acid**.

51.s: Amatol is a mixture of TNT and which of the following?
51.x: Amatol is TNT mixed with ammonium nitrate; it contains no nitroglycerine and is a high explosive, not a propellant.
n: Amatol contains no nitroglycerine. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
xa: **Dynamite** = **nitroglycerine** absorbed in **kieselguhr**.
**C-4** = **RDX** in a plastic matrix.
TNT is the **trinitrotoluene** in amatol.

51.s:
Assertion (A): Cordite contains nitroglycerine.
Reason (R): Cordite is a propellant.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
51.x: Both are true but R does not explain A: cordite is a nitroglycerine–nitrocellulose propellant; its use does not explain what it contains.
51.tq: Check whether R explains the content or only the use.
n: Cordite contains nitroglycerine. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
Cordite is a propellant. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 61-64]
xs: **Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A** — option **(2)**.
A is true: **Cordite** **contains nitroglycerine**.
R is true: cordite is a **propellant** — but its use does not explain its composition.
xa: **Dynamite** also contains **nitroglycerine** (in kieselguhr or sawdust).
⚠ **Amatol** has **no nitroglycerine**.
Nitroglycerine is also called **Nobel oil**.

51.s: By what other name is HMX known?
51.x: HMX is Octogen (High Melting Explosive); Cyclonite and Hexogen are RDX, HNIW is CL-20.

51.s:

53.s: S.I. unit of energy is
53.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer Screening
53.x: The SI unit of energy (and work) is the joule. Watt and kilowatt are units of power, and HP (horsepower) is a non-SI power unit.

53.s: Five bulbs each of 100 watt capacity in a tunnel are illuminated continuously for twenty hours. The consumption of electricity will be:
53.x: Energy = 5 × 100 W × 20 h = 10,000 Wh = 10 kWh = 10 units (1 unit = 1 kWh).

53.s: An electric bulb of 100 watt is used for 4 hours. The unit of electric energy used is –
53.x: Energy = 100 W × 4 h = 400 Wh = 0.4 kWh = 0.4 unit. 400 is the answer in watt-hours, not units.

53.s: The unit of electric power is
53.x: Power is the rate of using energy and is measured in watts (W); ampere is current, volt is potential difference and coulomb is charge.

53.s: Which one of the following is the value of 1 kWh of energy converted into joules?
Kilowatt Hour (kWh) represents the unit of which of the following?
53.x: A kilowatt-hour is power × time, so it is a unit of energy (1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J), not of power.

53.s: Which of the following combinations can be used as both primary and final energy resources?
53.src: APPSC Forest Section Officer General Studies & Mental Abilit
53.x: Coal, petroleum and natural gas are primary sources that can also be used directly as final energy (coal in industry and homes, gas as PNG/CNG, petroleum as fuel), so both pairs qualify.

53.s:
Consider the following statements about the energy intensity of GDP:
1. It is the energy used per unit of GDP.
2. A rising value shows growth decoupling from energy use.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
53.x: Energy intensity is energy used per unit of GDP; it is a falling, not rising, value that shows growth decoupling from energy use.
xa: **Peak demand** = highest power drawn in a **15-minute interval**.
⚠ **Energy shortage** in **MU**; **peak shortage** in **MW**.
NDC intensity targets (vs **2005**): **45% by 2030**, **47% by 2035**.

53.s: How is peak demand on an electricity grid defined?
o: The average power drawn over a full day
The highest power drawn in a 15-minute interval
The total electricity generated in a month
The maximum annual energy produced by renewable sources
53.x: Peak demand is the highest power drawn from the grid during a 15-minute interval.
53.tq: Distinguish instantaneous or interval-based peak power from aggregate energy generation.
xs: **Peak demand** is the **highest power drawn** on the grid in a **15-minute interval** — option **(2)**.
**Peak shortage** = unmet peak demand (**MW**); **energy shortage** = unmet energy requirement (**MU**).
xa: Record peak: **270.8 GW** (**May 2026**).
**Evening peak (6-11 p.m.)**: cooling demand after solar output drops.
NGAP: peak demand to reach **459 GW by 2035-36**.

53.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the four A's on which energy security rests?
53.x: The four A's are availability, accessibility, affordability and acceptability. Accumulation is not included.
53.tq: Find the look-alike term that is absent from the standard four-part formulation.
xs: **Accumulation** is not one of the four A's — option **(3)**.
Energy security rests on the **Four A's**: **availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability**.
xa: **Energy intensity** = energy used per unit of **GDP**; a falling value = growth **decoupling**.
**Peak demand** = highest power drawn in a **15-minute interval**.
⚠ **Energy shortage** in **MU**; **peak shortage** in **MW**.

53.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Energy shortage refers to unmet energy requirement and is expressed in MU.
2. Peak shortage refers to unmet peak demand and is expressed in MW.
Which of the above statement(s) is/are correct?
53.x: Energy shortage is unmet energy requirement (MU or %), while peak shortage is unmet peak demand (MW or %).
xa: **Peak demand** = highest power drawn in a **15-minute interval**.
Shortage fell from **4.2% (FY14)** to **0.03% (2025)**, **zero by Nov 2025**.
**Energy security**: availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability.

53.s: How many joules does one kilowatt-hour (kWh) of energy equal?
53.x: 1 kWh is a 1 kW device running for 1 hour = 1,000 W × 3,600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J; it is the 'unit' on electricity bills.
n: One kilowatt-hour is the energy consumed by a 1 kW device in 1 hour. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 50-57]
One kilowatt-hour equals 3.6 × 10⁶ joules. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 50-57]
Electricity cost is charged per unit in kWh. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 50-57]
xa: **Energy shortage** is counted in **MU** (million units); **peak shortage** in **MW**.
**Peak demand** = highest power drawn in a **15-minute interval**.
**Energy intensity** = energy used per unit of **GDP**.

53.s: In discussions of conventional energy resources, what does an energy crisis refer to?
o: A rise in electricity consumption during solar hours
A temporary fall in renewable-energy generation only
The danger that fossil fuels such as coal and petroleum may run out
A shortage limited to nuclear fuel imports
53.x: Energy crisis refers to the danger of exhaustion of fossil fuels such as coal and petroleum.
53.tq: Identify the underlying resource-depletion meaning rather than a short-term grid event.
xs: An **energy crisis** is the danger that **fossil fuels** like **coal and petroleum** will **run out** — option **(3)** (UKPSC **2006** key).
Fossil fuels still dominate: **coal** = **55%** of the energy mix.
xa: India has **17%** of world population but only **0.6% of gas**, **0.4% of oil** and **7% of coal** reserves.
Crude oil import dependence is **~88%**.
**Solar** is the second source after fossil fuels (UPPSC **2021**).

53.s:
Consider the following statements about energy terms:
1. Peak demand is the highest draw in a 15-minute interval.
2. A falling energy intensity of GDP shows growth decoupling.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
53.x: Both are correct: peak demand is measured over 15-minute intervals, and falling energy per unit GDP means decoupling.

53.s: Which of the following constitutes the maximum share in power generation in India?
53.src: APPSC Extension Officer Grade-I Common Paper General Studies
53.x: Thermal power (mainly coal) gives the largest share of India's electricity generation, over 70%; coal is about 55% of the energy mix.

53.s: There is strong positive correlation between Human Development Index and Per Capita Electricity Consumption in case of India because?
o: Status is recognized only through electricity consumption
Certain level of per capita energy consumption is needed to ensure minimally acceptable well being to the people
After reaching a minimum level of comfort, very high energy is required to marginally increase the comfort
The rich need electricity for comfort
53.src: APPSC Degree Lecturers General Studies & Mental Ability 2017
53.x: A certain minimum per-capita energy/electricity use is needed for a minimally acceptable level of well-being, which is why HDI rises with per-capita consumption at India's level.

53.s: Which one of the following is the best source of generating electricity in India from the viewpoint of sustainable development?
53.x: Of the options only hydroelectricity is a renewable source that does not use up its resource; coal, oil, gas and nuclear fuels are finite.

53.s: Which source supplies approximately 55% of India’s energy mix and over 74% of its power generation?
53.x: Coal supplies about 55% of the energy mix and more than 74% of power generation.
53.tq: Match the quantitative share with the correct fuel source.
xs: **Coal** supplies **55% of the energy mix** and **over 74% of power generation** (2025-26) — option **(1)**.
India is the world's **second-largest coal consumer**; coal leads installed capacity (**230 GW**).
xa: **Solar** is second in installed capacity (**157 GW, ~29%**) and the second source after fossil fuels (UPPSC **2021**).
**Nuclear** has only **8.78 GW** of installed capacity.
NITI scenario: coal's share of generation **~74% → 6-10%** by **2070**.

53.s: What is India's rank among the world's energy consumers?

xa: Coal = **55% of the energy mix**, over **74%** of power generation.
**Solar** is the second source after fossil fuels (UPPSC 2021).
Installed capacity: coal **230 GW**, solar **157 GW**, wind **56.8 GW**.

53.s: India’s per-capita electricity consumption increased from 957 kWh in FY 2014 to approximately what level in FY 2025?
53.x: Per-capita electricity consumption rose from 957 kWh in FY 2014 to 1,460 kWh in FY 2025.

xs: Per-capita electricity consumption rose from **957 kWh (FY 2014)** to **1,460 kWh (FY 2025)** — option **(1)**.
Older notes gave **1,181 kWh**, "about half the world average".
xa: Per-capita **generation** in **2024**: India **1,418 kWh**, China **7,097**, USA **12,701**.

IESS 2047 projects **2,911-2,924 kWh** per capita.

53.s: India’s per-capita energy consumption is approximately what fraction of the world average?

53.tq: Separate the current world-gap ratio from older references to one-half of the world average.
xs: India's per-capita energy is only **one-third of the world average** — option **(2)**.
⚠ "**About half** the world average" is an older figure for per-capita **electricity** (**1,181 kWh**).
xa: Consumption is **low** with a large **urban-rural disparity**.
Per-capita electricity ≈ **a fifth** of China's, **a ninth** of the USA's.

53.s: Why is the policy objective of raising per-capita electricity consumption linked to the Human Development Index?
o: Electricity consumption is unrelated to social development indicators
Higher electricity consumption automatically eliminates urban-rural disparity
A minimum level of per-capita consumption is needed for a minimally acceptable level of well-being
HDI measures only the availability of commercial energy
53.x: Per-capita electricity consumption acts as a proxy for energy use, and a certain minimum level is required to ensure a minimally acceptable level of well-being.
53.tq: Apply the development-indicator relationship to the policy objective.
xs: A **certain minimum level of per-capita consumption** is needed to ensure a **minimally acceptable level of well-being** — option **(3)** (APPSC **2016** key).
Per-capita electricity, a proxy for all energy, **correlates with HDI**, so policy aims to raise it.
xa: India's per-capita electricity rose from **957 kWh** to **1,460 kWh** (FY 2014 → FY 2025).
Consumption is **low per capita** with a large **urban-rural disparity**.
Energy security rests on the **Four A's**: availability, accessibility, affordability, acceptability.

53.s: Which of the following describes India's per-capita energy consumption?
o: Uniform across urban and rural areas
Low, with a large urban-rural disparity
High in rural areas and negligible in urban areas
53.x: India has low per-capita energy consumption with a large urban-rural gap.
xa: Per-capita electricity ≈ **a fifth** of China's and **a ninth** of the USA's.
Household electrification is **~99%**.
**Saubhagya** connected **26 million** households.

53.s: By 2040, which sector is projected to remain the largest consumer of energy in India?
53.x: Industry uses about half of India's electricity and stays the largest consumer by 2040, while cooking demand falls.

xa: Per-capita generation **2024**: India **1,418 kWh**, China **7,097**, USA **12,701**.
OECD average: a little above **8,000 kWh**.
Per-capita electricity consumption: **1,460 kWh** (FY **2025**).

53.s: Which of the following are the emerging drivers of India's peak electricity demand?

Only household lighting in rural areas
Only coal mining and railway electrification

53.x: Peak demand increased from 183 GW in December 2020 to more than 250 GW in April 2026, representing a rise of about 37%.

xs: Peak demand rose **37%** from **183 GW (Dec 2020)** to **over 250 GW (Apr 2026)** — option **(1)**.

xa: All-time high: **270.8 GW** in **May 2026**, ~**90 GW** above **2019**.

xs: **AT&C losses** fell from **22.62% (FY14)** to **15.04% (FY25)** — option **(1)**.

o: Renewable energy cannot contribute during daylight hours
Coal supplies less than one-tenth of power generation
The remaining deficit occurs mainly during non-solar evening hours
Electricity demand is highest only during solar hours

xs: The remaining deficit now falls in **non-solar evening hours**, so **storage** is needed — option **(3)**.

xa: NGAP storage need: **174 GW/888 GWh** = **94 GW** pumped storage + **80 GW** BESS.

Delhi uses **ToD tariffs** and smart meters for the **6-11 p.m.** peak.
