57.x: Anthracite is the highest-quality coal (highest carbon, least moisture).

57.s: Which one of the following types of coal contains a higher percentage of carbon than the rest?
57.x: Anthracite has the highest carbon percentage (80-95%), above bituminous, lignite and peat.

57.s: Which one of the following is the appropriate reason for considering the Gondwana rocks as most important of rock systems of India?
o: More than 90 per cent of limestone reserves of India are found in them
More than 90 per cent of India's coal reserves are found in them
More than 90 per cent of fertile black cotton soils are spread over them
None of the reasons given above is appropriate in this context
57.x: Gondwana rocks hold about 98% of India's coal reserves and 99% of production, which is why they are the most important rock system economically.

57.s: Which one of the following types of coal contains a higher percentage of Carbon than the rest?
57.x: Anthracite has the highest carbon content of all coal types (80-95%).

57.s: Which of these consists carbon?
57.x: Lignite (brown coal) is a carbon-bearing fuel; tin, silver and iron are metals.

57.s: Which one among the following statements regarding Indias coal is not correct?
o: 98% of reserves of coal in India belongs to Gondwana period.
Unknown amount of coal lies buried under the Ganga alluvium and the Deccan Trap.
Bituminous coal is found in both lower Gondwana rocks and in Tertiary rocks.
Gondwana coal is mainly found in the river valleys of Damodar, Mahanadi and Godavari.
57.x: The wrong statement is C: Tertiary coals are younger, low-carbon, high-moisture lignite/sub-bituminous types; bituminous coal is a Gondwana coal. 98% Gondwana share, buried coal under Ganga alluvium and Deccan Trap, and the Damodar-Mahanadi-Godavari valleys are correct.

57.s: Which of the following is a natural fuel?
57.x: Coal is a natural fossil fuel; petrol and diesel are refined from crude oil, and charcoal is made by heating wood.

57.s:
Consider the following statements.

I. The Damuda series of rock system cotain all the metallurgical coal in India.

II. Tamil Nadu is the chief producer of lignite coal in India.

III. Tertiary coal is mainly confined to the Peninsular India.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
57.x: I and II are correct: the Damuda (Lower Gondwana) series holds India's metallurgical coal, and Tamil Nadu (Neyveli) is the chief lignite producer. III is wrong: Tertiary coal is extra-peninsular (NE India, J&K).

57.s: Which of the following is not the property of a good fuel?
57.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer Screening
57.x: A good fuel has a HIGH calorific value; low moisture, harmless combustion products and controllable burning are desirable properties.

57.s: Which type of coal is most widely used and is also the coking grade?
57.x: Bituminous coal is the most widely used type and includes the coking grade.
57.tq: Identify the coal type by its use and industrial grade.
xs: **Bituminous** coal is the most widely used type and the **coking grade** — option **(1)**.
It has **60-80%** carbon (some notes say 40-80%) and occurs in **Jharkhand, Odisha, WB, Chhattisgarh, MP**.
**Lignite** is "brown coal" with **40-55%** carbon; **sub-bituminous** is used in power plants.
xa: **Jharia** is the largest **coking-coal** field.
Coking coal is imported mainly from **Australia**.

57.s: Which type of coal lies between bituminous coal and lignite in rank and is used in power plants?
57.x: Sub-bituminous coal ranks between bituminous coal and lignite and is used mainly in power plants.

57.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Gondwana coal?
o: It consists predominantly of Tertiary lignite deposits
It accounts for about 98% of India's coal reserves
It is about 250–300 million years old
It occurs in the Damodar, Mahanadi, Son and Godavari valleys
57.x: Gondwana coal is not Tertiary lignite; Tertiary deposits are younger and include lignite.
xa: Gondwana coal holds the **coking coal**.
⚠ **Gondwana** = 98%, coking; **Tertiary** = NE India, about 2% (e.g. **Mawlong**, Meghalaya).

57.s: Lignite, or brown coal, contains about how much carbon?
57.x: Lignite has only 25–35% carbon, below sub-bituminous coal (35–45%).

57.s: Gondwana coal accounts for about what share of India's coal reserves?
57.x: Gondwana coal (250–300 million years old) holds about 98% of reserves; Tertiary coal is only about 2%.

57.s: Which is the first stage in the transformation of wood into coal?
57.x: Peat is the first stage of wood turning into coal and has the lowest carbon.

57.s: Where is Tertiary coal mainly found in India?
o: North-East India and Jammu and Kashmir
57.x: Tertiary coal is younger, makes up about 2% of reserves and occurs mainly in the North-East and Jammu and Kashmir. Gondwana coal is in the peninsular valleys.

57.s: Which of the following set of places is associated with lignite occurrences mentioned in the classification?
57.x: Neyveli, Palana and Lakhimpur are identified with lignite occurrences. The other groups are associated with major coalfields of higher-rank coal regions.
57.tq: Recognise the lignite-location group instead of a group of Gondwana coalfields.
xs: **Neyveli, Palana and Lakhimpur** are lignite sites — option **(1)**.
**Korba, Raigarh** (Chhattisgarh), **Singrauli** (MP), **Talcher, Deogarh** (Odisha), **Raniganj** (WB), **Jharia, Bokaro, Giridih** (Jharkhand) are coalfields.
xa: Neyveli is in **Tamil Nadu**, Palana in **Rajasthan**, Lakhimpur in **Assam**.
Lignite: **40-55%** carbon, "**brown coal**"; reserves **47.295 BT**.

57.s: In terms of proven Coal reserves, the position of India amongst the countries of the World is
57.x: India has the world's fifth-largest coal reserves (after USA, Russia, Australia, China) but is the second-largest producer.

57.s: The State which produces largest amount of coal in India is
57.src: APPSC Welfare Organiser in AP Sainik Welfare (General Studie
57.x:
Jharkhand led coal output in the 2000s — now Odisha is the largest producer (239.40 MT, ~24%, 2023-24; Rajya Sabha USQ 36, 3 Feb 2025)
Odisha is now India's largest coal-producing State (239.40 MT, about 24% of output in 2023-24), ahead of Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand; Jharkhand was the older answer (now Odisha).

57.s: Rhur Basin of India is in
57.src: APPSC Forest Section Officer Screening Test General Studies
57.x: The Damodar Valley (Jharkhand-West Bengal) is called the 'Ruhr of India' for its coal (Jharia, Raniganj, Bokaro) and the iron-steel industry based on it; it holds about one-fourth of India's coal reserves.

57.s: Which of the following is not a coal field?
57.x: Mosabani (Jharkhand) is a copper mining centre; Raniganj, Umaria and Korba are coalfields.

57.s: Which of the following is NOT a coal field field??
o: Bokaro Answers with Explanations Q1 Answer:
57.x: Mosabani is a copper mine in Jharkhand, not a coalfield; Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro are major coalfields.

57.s: Which of the following is the largest coal area of India?
57.x: Jharia (Jharkhand, Damodar Valley) is among India's oldest and richest coalfields and its largest coking-coal field; Talcher and Yellandu are smaller.

57.s: Coal mines in Jharkhand are located at
57.x: Jharia is a major coalfield of Jharkhand; Jamshedpur is a steel city, Ranchi the capital and Lohardaga a bauxite area.

57.s: The first coal mine in India was opened at?
57.x: India's first coal mine was opened at Raniganj (West Bengal) in 1774.

57.s: Jharia [Jharkhand] is famous for
57.x: Jharia in Jharkhand is famous for its coal mines (best coking coal).

57.s: Jharia coalfield is particularly noted for which of the following?
o: Lignite deposits in the Satpura Basin
The first commercial coal mine in India
57.x: Jharia in Jharkhand is the largest coking-coal field and is situated in the Damodar Valley.
57.tq: Directly distinguish the coalfield by its special characteristic.
xs: **Jharia** (Jharkhand) is India's **largest coking-coal field** — option **(2)**.
The **first coal mine** was at **Raniganj** (**1774**); **Tertiary coal** is at **Mawlong** (Meghalaya) and Makum (Assam); **Satpura** is an MP basin.
xa: **Jharkhand** has India's **largest coal reserves**; other Jharkhand fields: **Bokaro, Giridih, Karanpura**.
The **Damodar valley** holds about **one-fourth** of India's coal.
Coking coal is a **Gondwana** coal; the MMDR amendment made it a **Critical and Strategic Mineral**.

57.s: Which of the following pairs of coalfields is correctly associated with Odisha?
57.x: Talcher and Deogarh, including the IB Valley, are coalfields of Odisha. Jharia and Bokaro are in Jharkhand, Korba and Raigarh in Chhattisgarh, and Singareni and Makum in Telangana and Assam respectively.
57.tq: Group coalfields by State and reject cross-State substitutions.
xs: **Talcher and Deogarh (IB Valley)** are Odisha coalfields — option **(4)**.
**Korba, Raigarh** = **Chhattisgarh**; **Jharia, Bokaro** = **Jharkhand**; **Singareni** = **Telangana** and **Makum** = **Assam**.
xa: **Talcher** lies on the **Brahmani**; it will host the first **gasification-based fertiliser plant** (due Dec **2027**).
APGENCO buys washed coal from **MCL's IB Valley Washery**.

57.s: In which State is the Mawlong coalfield, known for Tertiary coal, located?
57.x: Mawlong is in Meghalaya and is associated with Tertiary coal.
xa: **Tertiary coal**: NE India and J&K, about **2%** of reserves.
⚠ **Gondwana** = **98%**, coking coal; **Tertiary** = NE India, about 2%.
**Makum** (Assam) is another NE coalfield.

57.s: Which State leads India in lignite resources (estimated at 47.295 billion tonnes)?
57.x: Lignite resources are 47.295 billion tonnes, with Tamil Nadu (Neyveli) leading, followed by Rajasthan and Gujarat.
xa: Lignite ("**brown coal**") has **40-55%** carbon.
Other lignite sites: **Palana** (Rajasthan), **Lakhimpur** (Assam); **Barmer** (Rajasthan).

57.s: In which State is the Neyveli lignite field located?
57.x: Neyveli is in Tamil Nadu; Bokaro and Giridih are in Jharkhand and Raigarh in Chhattisgarh.
xa: Other Jharkhand fields: **Jharia** (largest coking coal), **Karanpura**.
**Korba** (Chhattisgarh) lies on the **Hasdeo** (Mahanadi basin).
**Singareni** is in **Telangana**.

57.s: Which State has the largest coal reserves in India?
57.x:
Many books: Jharkhand. Strictly: Odisha leads total resources; Jharkhand leads proved reserves (60,290 MT vs 55,010 MT, 1.4.2025).
Jharkhand was long taught as having the largest reserves — now Odisha has the largest total coal resources (100,975.78 MT, 1.4.2025, Ministry of Coal AR 2025-26)
Odisha has the largest coal resources (100,975.78 MT as on 1.4.2025), then Jharkhand (93,254.06 MT) and Chhattisgarh; Jharkhand still leads in proved (measured) reserves.

57.s: Where was India's first coal mine opened in 1774?
57.x: Raniganj in West Bengal had India's first coal mine in 1774.

57.s: As per GSI (1 April 2024), what are India's total coal resources?
57.x: GSI placed India's coal resources at 389.421 billion tonnes on 1 April 2024, with Jharkhand holding the most.

57.s: Which of the following coalfield – State pairs is correctly matched?
57.x: Korba (Hasdeo) is in Chhattisgarh; Talcher is in Odisha, Makum in Assam and Raniganj in West Bengal.

57.s: In which State is the Makum coalfield located?
57.x: Makum coalfield is in Assam; Mawlong (Tertiary coal) is in Meghalaya.

57.s: On which river valley does the Talcher coalfield of Odisha lie?
57.x: Talcher coalfield lies in the Brahmani valley in Odisha; Korba is on the Hasdeo in Chhattisgarh.

57.s: About what share of India's coal reserves lies in the Damodar valley?
57.x: The Damodar valley holds about one-fourth of India's coal reserves.

57.s: In which river valley does the Korba coalfield of Chhattisgarh lie?
57.x: Korba coalfield in Chhattisgarh lies in the Hasdeo valley.

57.s: Pneumoconiosis affects the workers who work mainly in :
57.x: Pneumoconiosis (e.g. black lung) is a lung disease caused by inhaling dust, mainly affecting coal miners.

57.s: In India, the steel production industry requires the import of
57.x: India has plenty of iron ore and non-coking coal but little good coking coal, so the steel industry imports coking coal (mainly from Australia).

57.s:
Which of the following is/are the characteristic/characteristics of Indian coal?

I. High ash content

II. Low sulphur content

III. Low ash fusion temperature
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
57.x: Indian coal has high ash (35-45%) and low sulphur, but a HIGH ash-fusion temperature (~1500°C), so I and II only.

57.s:
Consider the following statements:

I. Coal ash contains arsenic, lead and mercury.

II. Coal-fired power plants release sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen into the environment.

III. High ash content is observed in Indian coal.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
57.x: All three are correct: coal ash contains arsenic, lead and mercury; coal plants emit SO2 and NOx; Indian coal has high ash.

57.s:
Consider the following
Assertion (A) and
Reason (R) and choose the correct code:
Assertion (A): Coal washing results in increased generation efficiency and reduced investment costs. However, the use of washed coal in India is still limited.
Reason (R): The limited establishment of coal washeries may be attributed to the perception that coal washing by increasing the cost of electricity generation, would adversely impact the plants in terms of 'merit order' scheduling.
o: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) explains (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) does not explain (A).
57.x: Washing removes ash, raising efficiency and cutting transport and plant costs, yet washed coal use is limited because washing raises the fuel cost per unit and can push plants down the merit-order dispatch; R explains A.

57.s:
Consider the following statements about Indian coal:
1. It has high ash content.
2. It has high calorific value.
3. It has low sulphur content.
Which of the above statements are correct?
57.x: Indian coal generally has high ash, low calorific value, high ash-fusion temperature and low sulphur, so statement 2 is wrong.
xa: Low **washery** use worsens the quality problem.
APGENCO buys **washed coal** from **MCL's IB Valley Washery** for RTPP and Dr NTTPS.
Experts call for **CFB gasifiers** for high-ash coal.

57.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a problem affecting the Indian coal sector?
o: Excessive availability of high-quality domestic coking coal
57.x: The identified problems include poor quality, movement bottlenecks, low washery use, rising coking-coal imports and administrative issues. Excessive availability of high-quality domestic coking coal is not a stated problem.
57.tq: Find the option that reverses the sectoral problem described.
xs: **Excessive availability of high-quality domestic coking coal** is not a problem — option **(1)**; in fact **coking-coal imports are rising**.
Listed problems (BPSC key: all are problems): **poor quality**, **movement bottlenecks**, **low washery use**, **rising coking-coal imports**, **administrative issues**.
xa: Indian coal: **high ash (35-45%)**, low calorific value.
Coking coal comes mainly from **Australia**.

57.s: From which country does India mainly import coking coal?
57.x: Coking coal is imported mainly from Australia, whereas non-coking coal comes mainly from Indonesia and South Africa.
xa: Coking coal was made a **Critical and Strategic Mineral** under the MMDR amendment.
Gasification-substitutable imports (incl. coking coal) ≈ **₹2.77 lakh crore** in **FY2025**.

57.s: What is the usual ash content of Indian coal?
57.x: Indian coal has high ash (35–45%), low calorific value and low sulphur (about 0.5%).

57.s:
Consider the following statements about India's coal imports:
1. Coking coal is imported mainly from Australia.
2. Non-coking coal is imported mainly from Indonesia and South Africa.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
57.x: India imports coking coal mainly from Australia and non-coking coal from Indonesia and South Africa.

57.s: According to the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, how is the equity of Singareni Collieries Company Ltd. (SCCL) divided?
o: 51% with the Government of Telangana and 49% with the Government of India
49% with the Government of Telangana and 51% with the Government of India
51% with the Government of Telangana and 49% with the Government of Andhra Pradesh
49% with the Government of Telangana and 51% with the Government of Andhra Pradesh
57.src: APPSC Welfare Organiser in A.P Sainik Welfare Sub Service Ge
57.x: Under the AP Reorganisation Act 2014, SCCL's equity is 51% with the Government of Telangana and 49% with the Government of India (AP got no share).

57.s:
Consider the following statements relating to Coal India Limited.

I. It is designated as a ‘Maharatna’ company under the Ministry of Coal.

II. It is the single largest coal producing company in the world.

III. The headquarters of Coal India Limited is located at Ranchi (Jharkhand).
Which of the statement(s) given above is/are correct?
57.x: I and II are correct: Coal India Ltd is a Maharatna under the Ministry of Coal and the world's largest coal producer. III is wrong: its headquarters is Kolkata, not Ranchi.

57.s: India recorded coal production of how much in 2024–25, marking the first year in which production exceeded one billion tonnes?
57.x: India recorded 1,047.50 MT of coal production in 2024–25, the first time production crossed one billion tonnes.
57.tq: Use the exact production figure and distinguish it from the target and import figures.
xs: Coal output was **1,047.50 MT in 2024-25**, the first year above **1 billion tonnes** — option **(2)**.
xa: Imports fell **7.9%** to **243.62 MT**, saving about **$7.13 billion**.
By Aug 2025 output reached **381.749 MT**.
Coal meets about **55%** of commercial energy needs.

57.s: Coal accounts for approximately what share of India’s commercial energy needs?
57.x: Coal meets about 55% of India’s commercial energy needs.
57.tq: Distinguish the share in commercial energy needs from the higher share in power generation.
xs: Coal meets about **55%** of India's **commercial energy needs** — option **(3)**.
**About 70%** (some notes **71.4%**) is coal's share of **power generation**, not energy needs.

57.s: Which is the planning arm of Coal India Limited?
57.x: CMPDI is CIL's planning arm; SCCL is a Telangana-GoI company, not a CIL subsidiary.
xa: **SHAKTI policy** (**2017**) replaced the NCDP-2007 linkage regime.
Commercial coal auctions began in **2020**; **134 mines** sold after **12 rounds**.
**Coking coal** is now a **Critical and Strategic Mineral**.

57.s: What is the ownership pattern of Singareni Collieries Company Limited?
57.x: SCCL is owned 51% by Telangana and 49% by the Government of India.
57.tq: Watch for the reversed ownership percentages and the swapped governments.
xs: **SCCL** is owned **51% by Telangana** and **49% by the Government of India** — option **(1)**.
This follows the **AP Reorganisation Act Schedule**; existing coal linkages continue.
xa: **Singareni** coalfield is in **Telangana**.
APGENCO seeks **better coal from SCCL**.

57.s: How many subsidiaries does Coal India Ltd have?
57.x: Coal India Ltd, the world's largest coal producer, has 7 subsidiaries, with CMPDI as its planning arm.

57.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about India's coal producers?
o: Coal India Ltd is the world's largest coal producer
CMPDI is the planning arm of Coal India Ltd
SCCL is a subsidiary of Coal India Ltd
57.x: SCCL is owned 51% by Telangana and 49% by the Government of India; it is not a Coal India subsidiary.

57.s: What is India's coal production target for 2025-26?
57.x: After 1,047.50 MT in 2024-25, the 2025-26 target is 1,157 MT.

57.s: How are coal linkages given under the SHAKTI coal linkage policy (2017)?
57.x: SHAKTI, which replaced the NCDP-2007 regime, gives linkages through auction or tariff-based bidding.
xa: **199 mines** were allocated under the **CMSP Act 2015** and **MMDR Act 1957**.
Revenue-sharing **commercial auctions** began in **2020**.

57.s: In which year did revenue-sharing commercial coal auctions begin in India?
57.x: Revenue-sharing commercial coal auctions began in 2020.
57.tq: Place the auction mechanism in time against the nearby years of the CMSP Act, SHAKTI policy and later auction rounds.
xs: Revenue-sharing **commercial coal auctions** began in **2020** — option **(3)**.
**2015** is the **CMSP Act**; **2017** is **SHAKTI**; **2025** saw the **13th round** (**21 Aug 2025**).
xa: After **12 rounds**: **134 mines** sold, peak rated capacity **277.04 MTPA**.
**14th round**: mines to **Reliance Industries + Axis Energy**, first **UCG** clauses (2 May 2026).

57.s: The 14th round commercial coal mining agreements were the first to include clauses on which of the following?
57.x: The 14th-round agreements were the first to include underground coal gasification clauses.
57.tq: Link the special contractual clause with the correct technology rather than with the auction mechanism itself.
xs: 14th-round agreements were the first with **underground coal gasification (UCG)** clauses — option **(4)** (2 May 2026).
**Tariff-based bidding** belongs to the **SHAKTI** linkage policy (**2017**), not these clauses.
xa: **UCG** is an **in-situ** process: air/oxygen + steam injected into coal seams → syngas underground.
UCG uses deep, thin or unmineable coal; risk: **groundwater contamination**.
MoEFCC panel refused to waive the **300 m** minimum depth for UCG pilots.

57.s: Which mineral was declared a Critical and Strategic Mineral through an amendment to the MMDR framework, enabling the Centre to auction its leases?
57.x: Coking coal was declared a Critical and Strategic Mineral, allowing the Centre to auction its leases.
57.tq: Identify the specific coal variety and avoid substituting the broader category of coal.
xs: **Coking coal** was declared a **Critical and Strategic Mineral** — option **(3)**.
This lets the **Centre** auction its leases under the **MMDR** amendment.
xa: **Jharia** is the largest coking-coal field; coking coal is imported mainly from **Australia**.
Rising **coking-coal imports** are a listed coal-sector problem.
Coking coal is held in **Gondwana** coal.

57.s: After the Supreme Court cancelled 204 coal blocks in 2014, which Act provided for their auction?
o: Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957
57.x: The Coal Mines (Special Provisions) Act, 2015 was passed to auction the 204 blocks cancelled in 2014.

57.s: What did the MMDR Act amendment of March 2021 allow?
o: Auction of coal bed methane blocks
Sale of coal from captive mines
57.x: The March 2021 MMDR amendment permitted the sale of coal from captive mines.

57.s: When did the 13th round of commercial coal block auctions open?
57.x: The 13th round of revenue-sharing commercial auctions opened on 21 August 2025.

57.s: Which policy did the SHAKTI coal linkage policy (2017) replace?
57.x: SHAKTI (2017) replaced the New Coal Distribution Policy (NCDP) 2007 and gives linkages by auction or tariff-based bidding.

57.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about underground coal gasification (UCG)?
o: It is an in-situ process injecting air or oxygen and steam into coal seams to make syngas
The MoEFCC expert panel waived the 300 m minimum depth for UCG pilots
Groundwater contamination is a risk associated with it
It can use coal that is deep, thin or otherwise unmineable
57.x: The MoEFCC expert panel refused to waive the 300 m minimum depth.
xa: **CBM** ("sweet gas") is methane held in coal seams.
The **14th** commercial round had the first agreements with **UCG** clauses.
The **₹37,500 crore** gasification scheme drew **no bidders**.

57.s: Syngas produced by coal gasification can be used to run which type of power plant?
57.x: Syngas from coal gasification is burnt to run IGCC power plants.

57.s: Which of the following can be produced through coal gasification?
57.x: Ethanol and urea can be produced through coal gasification; nitroglycerine is not among the stated products.
xa: Urea comes via **ammonia for fertilisers**.
Other products: **SNG, methanol, hydrogen, DME, ammonium nitrate**.
**Talcher** will host the first gasification-based fertiliser plant (by Dec **2027**).

57.s: Which of the following pairs about coal bed methane (CBM) is correctly matched?
o: CBM in micropores of coal – Adsorbed form
CBM in micropores of coal – Free gas
CBM in joints of coal seams – Adsorbed form
'Sweet gas' label – Rich in heavier hydrocarbons
57.x: CBM lies free in the joints of coal seams and is adsorbed in the micropores of coal, so 'micropores – adsorbed form' is correct and the two joint/micropore pairs given the other way are wrong. CBM is called 'sweet gas'; it is not a gas rich in heavier hydrocarbons.

57.s: What does syngas produced by coal gasification mainly consist of?
57.x: Syngas is CO + H₂ + CH₄ + CO₂; ammonia is only a downstream product.

57.s: By what other name is coal bed methane (CBM) known?
57.x: CBM is called 'sweet gas'; it lies free in joints and adsorbed in micropores of coal.

57.s: For underground coal gasification, which minimum depth did the MoEFCC panel refuse to waive?
57.x: The MoEFCC panel refused to waive the 300 m minimum depth for in-situ UCG.

57.s: Which of the following CANNOT be produced through coal gasification?
57.x: Coal gasification yields products such as SNG, methanol, ethanol and urea; nitroglycerine cannot be made (UPSC 2025).

57.s: What is the outlay of the Scheme for Promotion of Surface Coal/Lignite Gasification approved on 13 May 2026?
57.x: The outlay is ₹37,500 crore, with incentives up to 20% of plant and machinery cost, capped at ₹5,000 crore per project.
xa: It targets about **75 MT** toward the **100 MT** goal; coal linkage tenure extended to **30 years**.
Earlier scheme (**2024**): **₹8,500 crore** for public and private projects.
Status (5 Sep 2026): **no bidders** so far.

57.s: Commercial coal blocks get a 50% rebate on revenue share if at least what share of their output goes to gasification?
57.x: Commercial blocks get a 50% rebate on revenue share if at least 10% of their output is used for gasification.
xa: **₹37,500 crore** scheme: incentive up to **20%** of plant cost, cap **₹5,000 crore** per project.
Mission goal: **100 MT** by **2030**.
14th-round mines carried the first **UCG** clauses.

57.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the ₹37,500-crore Surface Coal/Lignite Gasification scheme?
o: No bidders had turned up for it
Bid windows were planned every two months
It was withdrawn because the mission target had been achieved
57.x: The scheme drew no bidders and bid windows were planned every two months; it was not withdrawn.

57.s: The National Coal Gasification Mission aims to gasify how much coal by 2030?
57.x: The National Coal Gasification Mission has a target of gasifying 100 million tonnes of coal by 2030.
57.tq: Recall the mission target and distinguish it from the sub-target under the incentive scheme.
xs: The **National Coal Gasification Mission** aims to gasify **100 million tonnes** of coal by **2030** — option **(1)**.
**75 MT** is what the **₹37,500 crore** surface gasification scheme targets toward that goal.
xa: The Coal Ministry says the target will be met (**26 Apr 2026**).

58.s: The main component of Liquid Petroleum Gas (LPG) are :
58.x: LPG is the abbreviation or short form for Liquefied Petroleum Gas. Like all fossil fuels, it is a non-renewable source of energy. It is extracted from crude oil and natural gas. The main composition of LPG are hydrocarbons containing three or four carbon atoms. The normal components of LPG thus are propane (C3H8) and butane (C4H10). LPG mixtures contain a little more propane in winter and a little more butane during summer but, on average, the makeup is approximately 65% butane and 35% propane. Small concentrations of other hydrocarbons like ethane may also be present. Ethyl mercaptan is normally used as a stenching agent for smell.

60.s: A photoelectric cell is a device which :
o: converts light energy into electric energy
converts electric energy into light energy
60.x: A photoelectric cell converts light energy into electric energy. The photoelectric effect, where electricity is generated from a material when it absorbs light, was first discovered in 1887 by Heinrich Hertz. The photovoltaic effect is closely related to the photoelectric effect, with a critical difference. In the photoelectric effect, electrons are emitted into space. But, in the photovoltaic effect, electrons enter what we call the conduction band of the material. The photoelectric device can capture high-energy photons and generate a high-voltage output, while the photovoltaic cell can capture low-energy photons and generate a high-current output. This combination can increase the power output and efficiency of solar PV systems.

60.s: A device which converts electrical energy into mechanical energy is –
60.x: Electric motor is a device which converts electrical energy into mechanical energy. Electric motors involve rotating coils of wire which are driven by the magnetic force exerted by a magnetic field or an electric current.

60.s: Lightning can even burn a tree because it contains tremendous amount of
60.x: Lightning can even burn a tree because it contains tremendous amount of electrical energy. Lightning is an electrical discharge caused by imbalance between storm clouds and the ground, or within the clouds themselves.

60.s: A dynamo which is said to generate electricity actually acts as a :
60.x: A dynamo, which is also known as an electrical generator produces direct current through a commutator. It is basically a device which converts mechanical rotation into electric current according to Faraday's law.

60.s: The energy of wind is –
60.x: All moving things have kinetic energy. It is energy possessed by an object due to its motion or movement. Wind energy is the kinetic energy of air in motion. The kinetic energy of the wind (wind energy) can be converted into mechanical and electrical energy.

60.s: The photoelectric effect was discovered by :
60.x: Photoelectric effect is a phenomenon in which electrically charged particles are released from or within a material when it absorbs electromagnetic radiation. The effect is often defined as the emission of electron from a metal plate when light falls on it. This effect was discovered in 1887 by the German Physicist Heinrich Rudolf Hertz. This is also known as Hertz effect.

60.s: In wind power, which form of energy is converted into electrical energy?
60.x: The term wind energy or wind power describes the process by which the wind is used to generate mechanical power or electricity. Wind turbines convert the kinetic energy of the wind into mechanical power. This mechanical power can be used for specific tasks such as grinding grain or pumping water or a generator can convert this mechanical power into electricity.

60.s: Which of the following energy changes involves frictional force?
o: More than one of the above
60.x: Frictional forces apply in a static condition as well as in a moving condition. The respective co-efficient of friction are called static co-efficient and dynamic co-efficient. While in the static condition, there is no displacement i.e. no work done and hence no energy conversion. It is in the dynamic condition, there is movement against the frictional force that there is energy loss by way of heat. In other words, kinetic energy of movement is converted into heat. Energy conversion due to friction does not involve change in potential energy/chemical energy. Even when an object is falling in air, its potential energy first gets converted into kinetic energy and then heat or sound etc. In battery, its chemical energy is converted into electrical energy as well as heat but friction has nothing to do in such conversion.

60.s: Recently the term "pumped-storage hydropower" is actually and appropriately discussed in the context of which one of the following?
60.x: Pumped storage hydropower (PSH) is a type of hydroelectric energy storage. It is a configuration of two water reservoirs at different elevations that can generate power as water flows from one to the other (discharge) and passes through a turbine. The system also requires power to pump water back into the upper reservoir (recharge). PSH acts like a giant battery because it can store energy and release it when needed.

60.s: Recently, the term "pumped-storage hydropower" is actually and appropriately discussed in the context of which one of the following?
60.x: Pumped-storage hydropower (PSH) is a type of hydroelectric energy storage that uses water stored in two reservoirs at different elevations to generate electricity. When there is excess electricity available, such as during off-peak hours or from renewable sources like solar and wind, it is used to pump water from the lower reservoir to the upper reservoir. When there is a demand for electricity, the water is released from the upper reservoir back down to the lower reservoir, passing through turbines that generate electricity. PSH acts similarly to a giant battery, because it can store power and then release it when needed. Recently, the Ministry of Environment, Forest, and Climate Change (MoEFCC) has given the environment-related go-ahead to pumped storage hydropower projects with a capacity of 11.98 gigawatts (Gw) including Greenko Energy’s proposal for a 3.66 Gw project in Uttar Pradesh’s Sonbhadra district.

61.x: The atomic bomb works by uncontrolled nuclear fission; fusion is the principle of the hydrogen bomb.

61.s: Hydrogen bomb was developed by :
61.x: Edward Teller is called the father of the hydrogen bomb (first US test, November 1952). Oppenheimer led the fission bomb project.

61.s: What was the fissionable material used in the bombs dropped at Nagasaki (Japan) in the year 1945 ?
61.x: 'Fat Man', dropped on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945, used plutonium-239; 'Little Boy' at Hiroshima used U-235.

61.s: Which one of the following is incorrect?
o: Theory of evolution was propounded by Charles
The breaking apart of the nucleus of an atom is called
Dry ice is nothing but solid Carbon dioxide
Telephone was invented by Graham Bell
61.x: The breaking apart of a nucleus is fission, not fusion, so statement b is the incorrect one.

61.s: Hydrogen bomb is based on the principle of –
61.x: The hydrogen bomb works by uncontrolled fusion of deuterium and tritium into helium. Controlled reactions describe reactors, and fission describes the atom bomb.

61.s: The principle of atom bomb is based on –
61.x: The atom bomb relies on uncontrolled nuclear fission of uranium or plutonium. Fusion is the principle of the hydrogen bomb.

61.s: The working principle of atom bomb is nuclear fission of uranium and the working principle of hydrogen bomb is –
o: explosion of bomb involving hydrogen gas
61.x: The hydrogen bomb works by nuclear fusion of deuterium (and tritium) into helium, not by fission of thorium or chemical explosions.

61.s: Source of Energy from the Sun is :
61.x: The Sun's energy comes from nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core.

61.s: The difference between nuclear reactor and atom bomb is that :
o: There is no chain reaction in nuclear reactor whereas
The chain reaction in nuclear reactor is controlled
The chain reaction in nuclear reactor is not controlled
Atom bomb is based on nuclear fusion whereas in
61.x: Both a reactor and an atom bomb use a chain reaction; the difference is that in the reactor it is controlled.

61.s: The energy of Sun is released due to :
61.x: The Sun's energy is released by nuclear fusion (hydrogen into helium), not fission or oxidation-reduction.

61.s: Which statement is not associated with nuclear fission:
o: Source of energy in nuclear reactor that produces
Enormous energy is released in an atom bomb
61.x: Energy generation in stars comes from fusion, so it is not associated with fission. Fission is neutron-induced and powers reactors and the atom bomb.

61.s: Solar energy is due to
61.x: Solar energy comes from nuclear fusion in the Sun's core, not ionisation, fission or oxidation.

61.s: The first atom bomb was thrown over
61.x: The first atom bomb was dropped on Hiroshima (6 August 1945, Little Boy); Nagasaki followed on 9 August.

61.s: In which cities of Japan were atomic bomb dropped during Second World War?
61.x: Atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima (Little Boy) and Nagasaki (Fat Man) only.

61.s: Basic scientific principle behind a nuclear reactor is
61.x: A nuclear reactor runs on controlled nuclear fission. Uncontrolled fission is a bomb, and fusion power is still at the research stage.

61.s:
Consider the following statements.

I. The chain reaction process is used in nuclear bombs to release a vast amount of energy, but in nuclear reactors, there is no chain reaction.

II. In a nuclear reactor, the reaction is controlled, while in nuclear bombs, the reaction is uncontrolled.

III. In a nuclear reactor, all operating reactors are ‘critical’, while there is no question of ‘critically’ in case of a nuclear bomb.

IV. Nuclear reactors do not use moderators, while nuclear bombs use them.
Which of the above statements about operational principles of a nuclear reactor and a nuclear bomb is/are correct?
61.x: II and III are correct: a reactor's chain reaction is controlled and a running reactor is 'critical' (self-sustaining). I is wrong because reactors do use a chain reaction, and IV is wrong because reactors, not bombs, use moderators.

61.s: The source of energy of the sun is
61.x: The Sun runs on nuclear fusion (hydrogen into helium), not fission or photoelectric processes.

61.s: Hydrogen bomb is based on
61.x: The hydrogen bomb is based on nuclear fusion of deuterium and tritium, triggered by a fission bomb.

61.s: Nuclear fission is caused by the impact of
61.x: Fission starts when a neutron hits a heavy nucleus such as U-235, which splits and releases 2-3 more neutrons. Protons and electrons do not trigger it.

61.s: The difference between a nuclear reactor and atomic bomb is that
o: no chain reaction takes place in nuclear reactor is not controlled.
the chain reaction in nuclear reactor is controlled.
the chain reaction in nuclear reactor is not controlled.
no-chain reaction takes place in atomic bomb while it takes place in nuclear reactor.
61.x: In a reactor the chain reaction is controlled by moderators and control rods; in an atom bomb it is uncontrolled. Both involve chain reactions.

61.s: Hydrogen bomb is based on
61.x: The hydrogen bomb is based on nuclear fusion; the atom bomb is the one based on fission.

61.s: Which one of the following reactions is the main cause of the energy radiation from the sun?
61.x: The Sun radiates energy from fusion reactions (hydrogen into helium) in its core.

61.s: Which one of the following is not correct?
o: Theory of evolution was propounded by Charles Darwin.
The breaking apart of the nucleus of an atom is called fusion.
' Dry ice ' is nothing but solid carbon dioxide.
Telephone was invented by Graham Bell.
61.x: Breaking apart of a nucleus is fission, not fusion, so statement b is the incorrect one. Fusion is the joining of light nuclei.

61.s: What is the splitting of a heavy nucleus called?
61.x: Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus, while fusion is the joining of two light nuclei.
xa: ⚠ "Breaking apart of a nucleus is called fusion" is the **incorrect** statement (APPSC 2019).
All present-day nuclear electricity is from **fission**; fusion is still **R&D**.
**Atom bomb** = fission; **hydrogen bomb** = fusion.

61.s: Through which process is all present-day nuclear electricity generated?
61.x: Present-day reactors use fission; fusion occurs in the Sun and stars and fusion power is still at the R&D stage.
xa: **ITER** (Cadarache, France) is a **tokamak** fusion experiment.
**NIF** (USA) achieved the first fusion **ignition** in **Dec 2022** by laser.

61.s: How much energy per unit mass does nuclear fusion release compared with nuclear fission?
61.x: Fusion releases more energy per unit mass than fission, though it needs extremely high temperature and pressure.
xa: Fission needs a **neutron hit** and **critical mass**.
Fusion examples: **Sun and stars**, **hydrogen bomb**.
ITER is designed for **500 MW** output from **50 MW** input.

61.s: What initiates the fusion reaction in a hydrogen bomb?
61.x: A hydrogen bomb uses fusion triggered by a fission explosion; an atomic bomb is based on uncontrolled fission.
xa: **Hiroshima** (Little Boy) = **U-235**; **Nagasaki** (Fat Man) = **Pu-239**.
Fusion naturally powers the **Sun and stars**.
**Atomic Energy Act 1948** limited atomic energy to **peaceful uses**.

61.s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
61.x: The Hiroshima bomb, Little Boy, used U-235. The Nagasaki bomb, Fat Man, used Pu-239.
61.tq: Match the city, bomb name and fissile material as a three-part pair.
xs: **Hiroshima — Little Boy — U-235** is correct — so option **(3)**.
**Nagasaki** was **Fat Man** with **Pu-239**; options (1), (2), (4) mix these.
xa: Atom bomb = uncontrolled **fission**.
**Pu-239** is not natural — bred from **U-238**.
⚠ **Hiroshima = U-235**; **Nagasaki = Pu-239**.

61.s: What is the minimum mass of fissile material that can sustain a chain reaction called?
61.x: Critical mass is the minimum fissile mass for a chain reaction; criticality is the self-sustaining state itself.

61.s: The bomb 'Little Boy' dropped on Hiroshima used which fissile material?
61.x: Little Boy (Hiroshima) used U-235; Fat Man (Nagasaki) used Pu-239.

61.s: The mass number of a nucleus is :
o: the sum of the numbers of neutrons and protons
the total mass of neutrons and protons
always more than the atomic weight
always less than its atomic number
61.x: Mass number is the number of protons plus neutrons (the nucleon count). It is a count, not the total mass, and it is not always more or less than other quantities.

61.s: The atoms, in which the number of protons is same but the number of neutrons is different, are known as –
61.x: Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons are isotopes. Isobars share the mass number, isotones the neutron number.

61.s: The isoneutronic group, in the following, is :
61.x: Isoneutronic (isotone) nuclides have the same neutron number: 6C14 (14-6), 7N15 (15-7) and 8O16 (16-8) all have 8 neutrons. In option a the neutrons are 6, 7 and 8.

61.s: Isotopes is that nuclei of atomic nucleus in which –
o: Number of neutrons is same but number of protons is
Number of protons is same but number of neutrons is
Number of both protons and neutrons is same
Number of both protons and neutrons is different
61.x: Isotopes have the same number of protons (atomic number) but different numbers of neutrons. Same neutrons, different protons describes isotones.

61.s: The number of neutrons in the nucleus of plutonium nuclide (94Pu242) is :
61.x: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 242 - 94 = 148.

61.s: Constituents of atomic nucleus are –
61.x: The nucleus is made of protons and neutrons (the nucleons); electrons move around it in shells.

61.s: Isotopes are those atoms of the same element which have–
o: Atomic mass is same but atomic number is different
Atomic mass is different but atomic number is same
Atomic number and atoms mass both are same
61.x: Isotopes of an element have the same atomic number but a different atomic mass (mass number), because their neutron counts differ.

61.s: Isotopes of an element differ in :
61.x: Isotopes share the atomic number (protons and electrons) but differ in mass number, because their neutron counts differ.

61.s:
With reference to Isotopes, which of the following statements is/are correct?
1. Atoms with identical atomic numbers but different atomic mass numbers are known as isotopes.
2. Protium, Deuterium and Tritium are isotopes of carbon.
Select the correct answer from the code given below :
Code :
61.x: Statement 1 is correct: isotopes have the same atomic number and different mass numbers. Statement 2 is wrong: protium, deuterium and tritium are isotopes of hydrogen, not carbon.

61.s: The Nucleus of Helium has –
61.x: A helium nucleus (the alpha particle) has two protons and two neutrons.

61.s: Heavy water is that water –
o: The temperature of which is kept constant at 4°C
In which insoluble salts of Calcium and Potassium
In which isotopes takes place of Hydrogen
In which isotopes takes place of Oxygen
61.x: In heavy water (D2O) deuterium, an isotope of hydrogen, takes the place of ordinary hydrogen. Oxygen is unchanged.

61.s: The heaviest natural element is ?
61.x: Uranium (Z = 92) is the heaviest element found naturally in significant amounts. Gold, mercury and calcium are much lighter.

61.s: Atomic number of an atom gives the number of which of the following?
61.x: The atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus (equal to the electrons only in a neutral atom).

61.s: Isotopes of an element have ……… .
61.x: Isotopes of an element differ in their number of neutrons. They have the same atomic number and the same chemical properties.

61.s: Electrons in the highest energy level of an atom are called
61.x: Electrons in the outermost (highest energy) shell are valence electrons. 'Valence' or 'orbital' protons do not exist.

61.s: An element has an atomic weight of W and an atomic number of N. The number of protons in the nucleous of its atom is
61.x: The number of protons equals the atomic number, N. W is the mass number and W - N gives the neutrons.

61.s: Atomic mass of an element is equal to the sum of number of
61.x: The atomic mass (mass number) of an element is the sum of its protons and neutrons; electrons add almost nothing.

61.s: Atoms of different elements have
o: same atomic number and same electronic configuration.
different atomic number and same electronic configuration.
different atomic number and different number of valence electrons.
same number of electrons and neutrons.
61.x: Atoms of different elements have different atomic numbers and so different electronic configurations and numbers of valence electrons.

61.s: Mass number is always equal to ……..
o: sum of number of protons and number of electrons
sum of number of protons and number of neutrons
61.x: Mass number is always the sum of protons and neutrons.

61.s: Which one among the following is the most appropriate statement with respect to the atomic weight of an element?
o: The atomic weight of an element is the sum total of the number of protons and neutrons present in the atom of an element.
Unlike mass number, the atomic weight of an element can be a fraction.
The atomic weight of an element is a whole number.
The atomic weight of all the atoms in an element is the same.
61.x: Atomic weight is the average mass of an element's isotopes, so it can be a fraction (chlorine 35.5), whereas the mass number is always a whole number.

61.s: The atoms of the elements having same difference between mass number and atomic number are called …………… .
61.x: Mass number minus atomic number gives the neutrons; atoms with the same neutron number are isotones.

61.s: Isobars have …… .
o: same mass numbers but different atomic numbers.
different mass numbers but same atomic numbers.
61.x: Isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers (3H and 3He).

61.s: Scattering of α-particles by a thin gold foil suggests the presence of
o: positively charged nucleus at the centre of an atom
61.x: Most alpha particles passed through the gold foil but a few bounced back, showing a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at the centre of the atom (Rutherford).

61.s: The most of the mass of the atom can be found in
61.x: Protons and neutrons in the nucleus carry almost all the atom's mass; electrons are about 1/1837 of a proton.

61.s: An atom has 7 electrons in its M-shell and contains 18 neutrons in its nucleus. What is its mass number?
61.x: 7 electrons in the M-shell means 2 + 8 + 7 = 17 electrons, so 17 protons. Mass number = 17 + 18 = 35.

61.s: The force of attraction between an electron revolving around the nucleus and the nucleus is an … force.
61.x: The negatively charged electron and the positively charged nucleus attract by the electric (electrostatic) force; gravity is negligible at that scale.

61.s: Neutron is a fundamental particle carrying
o: a charge of + 1 and mass of 1 unit.
no charge and a mass of 1 unit.
a charge of - 1 and a mass of 1 unit.
61.x: A neutron has no charge and a mass of about 1 atomic mass unit (slightly more than a proton).

61.s: Charge on proton is equal to the charge on ………… .
61.x: A positron carries +1 charge, the same as a proton. The electron is negative, the neutron neutral and the alpha particle +2.

61.s: Chemical properties of Isotopes
61.x: Isotopes have the same number of protons and electrons, so their chemical properties must be the same; only physical properties such as mass differ.

61.s:
Which of the following statements with regard to isotopes and isobars is/are correct?

I. Isotopes have same mass number.

II. Isobars have same atomic number.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
61.x: Both statements are reversed: isotopes share the atomic number (not the mass number) and isobars share the mass number (not the atomic number). So neither is correct.

61.s: An atom of carbon has 6 protons. Its mass number is 12. How many neutrons are present in an atom of carbon?
61.x: Neutrons = mass number - protons = 12 - 6 = 6.

61.s: The number of electrons and neutrons in an element is 18 and 20 respectively. Its mass number is
61.x: A neutral atom has as many protons as electrons (18), so the mass number = 18 + 20 = 38.

61.s: Which one of the following statements about the properties of neutrons is not correct?
o: Neutron mass is almost equal to proton mass
Neutrons are located inside the atomic nuclei
Neutrons revolve around the atomic nuclei
61.x: Neutrons sit inside the nucleus; they do not revolve around it (electrons do). Their mass is almost equal to a proton's and they have zero charge.

61.s: What are ³H and ⁴He, each having two neutrons, called?
61.x: Nuclides with the same number of neutrons are isotones; ³H and ⁴He both have 2 neutrons.
n: ³H and ⁴He are isotones. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
³H and ⁴He each have two neutrons. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
¹⁴C, ¹⁵N, and ¹⁶O are isotones. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
¹⁴C, ¹⁵N, and ¹⁶O each have eight neutrons. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
xa: Isotones are also called **isoneutronic species**.
Isotones differ in **atomic numbers** and **mass numbers**.
**Tritium** = 1 proton + 2 neutrons; half-life **12.3 years**.

61.s: Which element is bombarded with neutrons to produce tritium?
61.x: Tritium (1 proton + 2 neutrons) is produced by bombarding lithium with neutrons.
xa: Tritium has **1 proton + 2 neutrons** and is a **fusion fuel**.
Fusion joins **two light nuclei** — as in the **Sun and stars**.

61.s: What are atoms having the same mass number but different atomic numbers called?
61.x: Isobars share mass number but differ in atomic number; isotopes share atomic number but differ in mass number.
n: An isotope has the same atomic number and different mass numbers. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
An isobar has the same mass number and different atomic numbers. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 39-42]
xa: Isotope example: **¹H, ²H, ³H** — ²H = **deuterium**, ³H = **tritium**.
Isobar example: **³H** and **³He**.
**Isotones** share the **number of neutrons**.

61.s: The most common method Uranium enrichment is?
61.src: APPSC Teaching Staff of the Department of Technical Educatio
61.x: Uranium (as UF6 gas) is enriched mostly in gas centrifuges, which separate U-235 from the slightly heavier U-238. Distillation, ionisation and calcification are not used.

61.s: The fuel used in the nuclear reactors is
61.x: Uranium (U-235) is the fuel of nuclear reactors. Thorium is only fertile and must first be bred into U-233; radium is not a reactor fuel and 'nuclear water' does not exist.

61.s: Material most commonly used in nuclear power plants is
61.x: Uranium-235 is the fissile fuel most commonly used in nuclear power plants. Plutonium is used in fewer reactors, thorium is only fertile and radium is not a fuel.

61.s: Which of the following radio active elements is used to make nuclear fission reaction?
61.x: Uranium (its fissile isotope U-235) is the element split in nuclear fission reactors and bombs. Thorium is fertile and must first become U-233; barium is a fission product, not a fuel.

61.s: Which nuclear fuel is produced when thorium is bombarded with neutrons?
61.x: Th-232 is fertile; when it absorbs a neutron it turns into fissile Uranium-233. Hard water, hydrogen sulphide and heavy water are not nuclear fuels.

61.s: What nuclear fuel does bombarding Thorium with neutrons produce?
61.x: Bombarding Thorium-232 with neutrons converts it into fissile Uranium-233, the basis of India's thorium fuel cycle. The other options are not nuclear fuels.

61.s:
Consider the following statements with reference to the enrichment of Uranium:

I. Uranium enrichment refers to increasing the percentage of U-238 (the fissile isotope) through the process of isotope separation.

II. Weapons-grade Uranium has to be enriched to a maximum of 20 percent of the fissile isotope.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
61.x: Statement I is wrong: enrichment raises the share of U-235, the fissile isotope, not U-238 (which is fertile). Statement II is wrong: 20% is the ceiling for research reactors, while weapons-grade uranium is about 90% U-235. So neither is correct.

61.s: Which one of the following elements is essential for the construction of nuclear reactors?
61.x: Zirconium alloys clad the fuel rods because they resist corrosion and absorb very few neutrons. Cobalt, nickel and tungsten are not essential reactor materials.

61.s: Which Uranium isotope is used in nuclear power plants to produce electricity?
61.x: U-235 is the fissile isotope burnt in nuclear power plants; natural uranium has only about 0.7% of it. U-233 is bred from thorium, while U-234 and U-239 are not used as fuel.

61.s: Identify the mineral not associated with atomic power –
61.x: Chromium has no role in atomic power. Monazite is the ore of thorium, thorium is a fertile fuel and beryllium (oxide) is a moderator and a prescribed atomic substance.

61.s: Which fuel is used by Nuclear reactors in India ?
61.x: Indian PHWRs burn natural uranium, which is about 99.3% U-238 with 0.7% U-235, so U-238 is the only printed option that fits. U-270 and U-500 do not exist and gasohol is a motor fuel.

61.s: Which of the following element is not included as a nuclear fuel–
61.x: Cadmium is not a fuel: it absorbs neutrons and is used in control rods. Thorium, plutonium and uranium are nuclear fuels (thorium after breeding).

61.s: Enriched Uranium is –
o: Uranium sticks laid in particular shell
Natural uranium in which radioactive U235 isotope is
mixture of natural uranium and thorium
61.x: Enriched uranium is natural uranium in which the share of the U-235 isotope has been raised by isotope separation. It is not a thorium mixture or coated sticks.

61.s: Which is not used as Atomic fuel?
61.x: Lead is not a nuclear fuel. Uranium and plutonium are fissile, and thorium is fertile and can be bred into U-233.

61.s: Which of the following is not a fuel element?
61.x: Helium is an inert gas and not a nuclear fuel element. Uranium and thorium are nuclear fuels; radium is radioactive but the clear odd one out is helium.

61.s: Which one of the following can not be used as a nuclear fuel?
61.x: Calcium is not a nuclear fuel. Uranium-235 and plutonium-239 are fissile, and thorium is bred into U-233.

61.s: Which metal can be used for producing electricity?
61.x: Uranium is the metal used to produce electricity, as nuclear fuel in power plants. Iron, copper and aluminium only carry or build things.

61.s: Which of the following uranium isotope is used in nuclear reactor for generation of electricity?
61.x: U-235 is the fissile uranium isotope used to generate electricity. U-233 is bred from thorium, while U-334 does not exist and U-239 is not a fuel.

61.s: Which one of the following is a good nuclear fuel?
61.x: Plutonium-239 is fissile, so it is a good nuclear fuel. U-238 is only fertile (it must first become Pu-239), neptunium is not a fuel and 'thorium-236' is not the fertile Th-232. (The old app notes said the APPSC 2007 key was U-238; that key was not verified and is factually wrong.)

61.s: Which of the following is wrongly matched?
o: U-238 – Fissile fuel of Stage III and KAMINI
U-233 – Fissile fuel of Stage III and KAMINI
Pu-239 – Fissile isotope produced from U-238 by neutron absorption
U-235 – Fissile isotope present in natural uranium
61.x: U-238 is the fertile isotope converted into Pu-239; the fuel of Stage III and KAMINI is U-233.
xa: **Th-232** (fertile) → **U-233** in FBR blankets.
**KAMINI** = world's only operating **U-233** reactor.

61.s: What does enrichment of uranium refer to?
o: Removing all radioactive isotopes from natural uranium
Increasing the proportion of U-238 through chemical separation
Increasing the proportion of U-235 through isotope separation
61.x: Enrichment raises the share of U-235, the fissile isotope, by isotope separation; it does not increase U-238.
61.tq: Discriminate between the fissile isotope U-235 and the fertile isotope U-238.
xs: **Enrichment** = raising the share of **U-235** by **isotope separation** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It does not raise **U-238** or convert U-235 into thorium.
xa: ⚠ APPSC-G1 2022 trap: the answer was "**Neither I nor II**" (both statements false).
**LWRs** use **low-enriched uranium (3-5% U-235)**; weapons-grade ≈ **90%**.
Natural uranium has only **0.72%** U-235.

61.s: Which one of the following is NOT a nuclear fuel but may serve as a moderator, coolant or absorber in a reactor?
61.x: Graphite is a reactor moderator, not a nuclear fuel. U-235, Pu-239 and U-233 are fissile fuels.
61.tq: Find the non-fuel by separating reactor-support materials from fissile isotopes.
xs: **Graphite** is a **moderator**, not a nuclear fuel — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Pu-239**, **U-235** and **U-233** are all **fissile fuels**.
xa: Other non-fuels: **heavy water, sodium, boron, cadmium, zirconium**.
**Control rods** (boron, cadmium) absorb neutrons.
**Liquid sodium** is the **FBR** coolant.

61.s: What percentage of natural uranium is U-235?
61.x: Fissile U-235 is only 0.72% of natural uranium; fertile U-238 is 99.28%.

61.s: To what level of U-235 must uranium be enriched for light water reactors?
61.x: LWRs need 3–5% U-235, above the natural 0.72%.

61.s: U-238 is a fertile isotope. Into which fissile material is it converted?
61.x: U-238 absorbs a neutron and becomes fissile Pu-239; Th-232 becomes U-233.

61.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about nuclear isotopes?
61.x: U-238 is fertile, not fissile; the fissile fuel bred from it is Pu-239.

61.s: Which one of the following is not radioactive ?
61.x: Zirconium (Z = 40) is not radioactive. Astatine and francium are heavy radioactive elements and tritium is a radioactive isotope of hydrogen.

61.s: Radioactive substance emits –
61.x: An unstable nucleus can emit alpha, beta and gamma radiation, so all three.

61.s: Emission of β-particle from an atom
o: increases the number of protons in the atom.
increases the number of neutrons in the atom.
decreases the number of proton in the atom.
does not change the number of neutrons and protons in an atom.
61.x: In beta-minus emission a neutron changes into a proton and an electron, which is emitted, so the number of protons rises by one.

61.s: What is end product of nuclear fission of Uranium?
61.x:
Printed key / books: Lead (end of the uranium decay series). Strictly, nuclear fission of uranium yields barium, krypton and other fission fragments, not lead (PMF S&T Part 4 p.24).
Lead is the stable end product of uranium's radioactive decay series (U-238 to Pb-206), which is the reading the key takes. Fission itself splits uranium into lighter nuclei such as barium and krypton; radium and thorium are intermediate decay products and plutonium is bred from U-238.

61.s: Which of the following is not a radioactive series?
61.src: APPSC Degree Lecturers General Studies & Mental Ability 2017
61.x: There is no 'carbon series'. Thorium, actinium and uranium are natural radioactive decay series, and neptunium is an artificial series.

61.s: The alpha particle carries two positive charges. Its mass is very nearly equal to that of:
o: Sum of masses of two positrons and two neutrons
Two positrons, as each positron carries a single positive charge
61.x: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus (2 protons + 2 neutrons), so its mass is almost that of a helium atom; electrons weigh very little. Two protons alone would be only half that mass.

61.s: Which of the following particles has zero charge?
61.x: The neutrino has zero charge (and almost no mass). The positron is +1, the electron -1 and the alpha particle +2.

61.s: Which of the following is not a sub-atomic particle?
61.x: The basic sub-atomic particles are the neutron, proton and electron. A deuteron is the nucleus of deuterium (a proton plus a neutron), not a basic sub-atomic particle.

61.s: Which of the following carries a negative charge?
61.x: Beta particles are fast electrons and carry a negative charge. Alpha particles are positive, while X-rays and gamma rays are uncharged radiation.

61.s: The half-life of a radioactive substance is 10 days; it means there will be :
o: complete decay of substance in 20 days
complete decay of substance in 40 days
decay of 3/4 part of substance in 20 days
decay of 1/4 part of substance in 5 days
61.x: After one half-life (10 days) half remains, after two (20 days) a quarter remains, so 3/4 has decayed in 20 days. A substance never decays completely.

61.s: The half-life of a radioactive element is 5 years then the fraction of the radioactive substance that remains after 20 years is –
61.x: 20 years is 4 half-lives of 5 years, so (1/2)^4 = 1/16 of the substance remains.

61.s: The alpha particle carries two positive charges. Its mass is very nearly equal to that of –
o: Nucleus of an atom of helium
Sum of masses of two positrons and two neutrons
Two positrons, as each positron carries a single

Half of its radioactive nuclei to decay

61.s: A moderator is used in nuclear reactors in order to
o: slow down the speed of neutrons
61.src: APPSC Forest Beat Officer & Assistant Beat Officer Screening
61.x: A moderator slows fast neutrons to thermal speed so that U-235 can capture them and fission. It does not add, absorb or accelerate neutrons; absorbing is the job of control rods.

61.s: ___ is used as a moderator in nuclear reactors.
61.x: Heavy water (D2O) is a moderator: it slows neutrons while absorbing very few of them. Hydrogen peroxide, dihydrogen and CFCs are not moderators.

61.s: Which one of the following is used as moderator in a nuclear reactor ?
61.x:
Printed key / most books: (b) Heavy water. Strictly, (d) ordinary water is also a moderator, in light-water reactors (PMF S&T Part 4 p.38).
Heavy water slows neutrons without absorbing many, so it is the classic moderator. Ordinary (light) water is a moderator too, in PWRs and BWRs, which is why the book lists '(b) & (d)'. Thorium and radium are not moderators.

61.s: Which one of the following is used as a moderator in the nuclear reactor?
61.x:
Printed key / most books: (b) Graphite. Strictly, (d) ordinary water is also a moderator, in light-water reactors (PMF S&T Part 4 p.38).
Graphite slows neutrons and is a standard moderator. Ordinary water is also a moderator in light-water reactors, which is why the book prints '(b) & (d)'. Thorium and radium are not moderators.

61.s: Graphite is used in the nuclear reactor as –
61.x: Graphite slows fast neutrons, so it serves as a moderator; it is not the fuel. Its lubricant use is outside reactors.

61.s: The moderator used in nuclear reactor is :
61.x: Heavy water, D2O (deuterium oxide), is the moderator. U2O, Na2O and Cl2O are not moderators.

61.s: What is the function of moderator in a nuclear reactor?
61.src: APPSC Forest Subordinate Service (Thanedar) Paper-II General
61.x: A moderator slows down neutrons so that they can cause further fission. Absorbing heat is the coolant's job; control rods regulate the rate.

61.s: What happens if the control rods are not used in a nuclear reactor?
o: Chain process would go out of bounds
The reactor will be slow to act
The reactor will continue to work as it is
61.x: Control rods absorb surplus neutrons; without them the chain reaction would go out of bounds rather than stop or slow down.

61.s: The substance used as moderator and coolant both, in nuclear reactors is :
61.x:
Printed key / most books: (a) Ordinary water. Strictly, (b) heavy water is also both moderator and coolant, in PHWRs (PMF S&T Part 4 p.43-44).
Ordinary (light) water is both the moderator and the coolant in PWRs and BWRs. Heavy water does both jobs in PHWRs, which is why the book prints '(a) & (b)'. Liquid ammonia and liquid hydrogen are neither.

61.s: Heavy water is a type of –
61.x: Heavy water is chiefly a moderator that slows neutrons; in PHWRs it also acts as coolant. It is not an ore or a fuel.

61.s: Heavy water is used as a moderator in a nuclear reactor. The function of the moderator is
o: to control the energy released in the reactor.
to absorb neutrons and stop the chain reaction.
to slow down the neutrons to thermal energy.

o: chain reaction will go out of control.
there will be impact on nuclear reactor.

61.s: The function of heavy water in a nuclear reactor is to?
o: Slow down the speed of neutrons.
61.x: Heavy water acts mainly as a moderator: it slows fast neutrons to thermal speed while absorbing very few. It does not speed neutrons up or stop the reaction. (In PHWRs it also cools, but 'cool down the reactor' is not the key.)

61.s: The function of heavy water in a nuclear reactor is to
o: Slow down the speed of neutrons
61.x: Heavy water is used as a moderator to slow down the neutrons produced in fission so that the chain reaction can be sustained. It does not increase their speed or stop the reaction.

61.s: In Light Water Reactors, which account for over 85% of world nuclear capacity, what role does light water play?

61.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the sequence of India's three-stage nuclear power programme?

61.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a bottleneck affecting the progression towards Stage III?

61.s:
With reference to India, consider the following statements :
1. Monazite is a source of rare earths.
2. Monazite contains thorium.
3. Monazite occurs naturally in the entire Indian coastal sands in India.
4. In India, Government bodies only can process or export monazite.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
61.x: Monazite is a complex reddish-brown phosphate of thorium and rare earth minerals [(Ce, La, Nd, Th, Y) PO4] and this is radioactive in nature. In India, monazite is the principal source of rare earths and thorium. Monazite bearing economic heavy mineral deposits are found along the coastal and inland placer sands of the country. However, monazite is not found in entire Indian coastal sands. Atomic Minerals Directorate for Exploration and Research (AMD), a constituent unit of Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) has so far established 13.15 million tonnes (as per the latest available estimates) of monazite contained in deposits in the coastal beach placer and teri/red sands in parts of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat and in the inland alluvium in parts of Jharkhand, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu. These deposits have been formed naturally due to littoral action of sea waves coupled with wind action. In India, private firms are restricted from processing or exporting monazite. Monazite is a strategic mineral and cannot be sold in commercial market. It is a prescribed substance to be handled by the DAE. IREL (Indian Rare Earths Limited), a Government of India Undertaking under the DAE and KMML (The Kerala Minerals and Metals Ltd.), a Kerala State Government Undertaking, are actively engaged in mining and processing of beach sand minerals from placer deposits. IREL is the only entity processing monazite to produce thorium and rare earth (RE) compounds.

62.s: Kalpakkam is famous–
62.x: Kalpakkam (Chennai, Tamil Nadu) is known for its nuclear plants and affiliated research installations. These include the Madras Atomic Power Station (MAPS), a nuclear power plant, and the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR- established in 1971), an affiliate of the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) and the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC). Madras Atomic Power Station (MAPS) is a comprehensive nuclear power production, fuel reprocessing, and waste treatment facility that includes plutonium fuel fabrication for fast breeder reactors (FBRs). It is also India's first fully indigenously constructed nuclear power station, with two units each generating 220 MWe of electricity (operated by NPCIL). Kalpakkam is also home to India's first large scale fast breeder reactor of 500 MWe (under construction) called the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor operated by BHAVINI and will also be the site of first two FBR-600 commercial fast breeder reactors. A beachhead at Kalpakkam also hosts India's first indigenous pressurised (light) water reactor (PWR). The 80 MWe reactor was developed by Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) as the land-based prototype of the nuclear power unit for India's nuclear submarines.

2. Photovoltaics generates Alternating Current (AC), while Solar Thermal generates Direct Current (DC).
3. India has manufacturing base for Solar Thermal technology, but not for Photovoltaics.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
65.x: Statement 1 is correct: Photovoltaic (PV) technology converts sunlight directly into electricity using semiconductors such as silicon, representing a direct conversion of solar energy into electrical energy. In contrast, solar thermal technology concentrates sunlight using mirrors or lenses to generate heat, which is then used to drive turbines and produce electricity, making it an indirect process. Statement 2 is incorrect: Photovoltaic systems produce Direct Current (DC), which is typically converted into Alternating Current (AC) using an inverter for practical and grid applications. Solar thermal systems, on the other hand, generate heat energy that is used to run turbines and produce AC electricity. Statement 3 is incorrect: India possesses a manufacturing base for both solar thermal technology and photovoltaic systems.

A photovoltaic cell is the basic unit of the system where the photovoltaic effect is utilized to produce electricity from light energy. Silicon is most widely used semiconductor material for constructing photovoltaic cell.

2. Photovoltaics generates Alternating Current (AC), while Solar Thermal generates Direct Current (DC).
3. India has manufacturing base for Solar Thermal Technology, but not for Photovoltaics.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
65.x: Photovoltaics refers to a technology which converts light into electricity using semiconducting materials that exhibit photovoltaic effect. Photovoltaic (solar) cells produce direct current electricity from sunlight. On the other hand, Solar Thermal Technology works on the principle of converting solar energy into heat energy by absorbing it which can be further used for electricity generation. In March, 2013 Ministry of New and Renewable Energy, Government of India informed that India has capacity of generating 2000 MW electricity through solar photovoltaic modules. This clarifies that India has infrastructure for photovoltaic technology.

65.s: Which one of the following elements is used in solar cells?
65.x: Solar cells are the components of solar arrays that convert radiant light from the sun into electricity that is then used to power electrical devices. Solar cells contain materials with semiconducting properties in which their electrons become excited and turned into an electrical current when struck by sunlight. While there are a dozen of variation of solar cells, the two most common types are those made of crystalline silicon (both monocrystalline and polycrystalline) and those made with what is called thin film technology. The majority (90 %) of the solar cells on the market today are made of silicon.

65.s: Which of the following is the value of solar constant ?
65.x: The 'solar constant' is defined as the amount of solar energy received per unit surface at a distance of one astronomical unit (the average distance of Earth's orbit) from the Sun. The total solar irradiance (TSI) reaching Earth per unit area was originally thought to be a fixed value and was referred to as the solar constant. Over the years, measurement of this quantity by various techniques yielded values that were quite different from one another. Satellite TSI measurements have enabled significant convergence in scientific consensus on the TSI value, which observations from the currently operational NASA Solar Radiation and Climate Experiment (SORCE) have determined to be 1,361 watts per square meter (W/m2). However, this value is not constant, but actually varies with time depending on solar activity, which is reflected in the counts of sunspots. It changes by ~0.1% in an 11-year solar cycle. Prior to the measurements obtained by the SORCE, the TSI value was estimated at 1366 W/m2. The current TSI value from the TSIS-1 is 1361.6 ± 0.3 W/m2 for the 2019 solar minimum. Hence, option (b) is the closest answer (1.4 kW/m2 = 1400 W/m2).

65.s: Which is the dominant solar-cell technology in the market?

67.s: Most of the sources of energy we use, represent stored solar energy. Which of the following is NOT ultimately derived from the Sun's energy?
67.x: & (b) Geothermal energy is heat that is generated within the Earth. It comes from heat generated during the original formation of the planet and the radioactive decay of materials. This thermal energy is stored in rocks and fluids in the centre of the earth. Nuclear energy is a form of energy released from the nucleus, the core of atoms, made up of protons and neutrons. This source of energy can be produced in two ways : fission – when nuclei of atoms split into several parts; or fusion – when nuclei fuse together. 67.s:
It is possible to produce algae-based biofuels, but what is/are the likely limitation(s) of developing countries in promoting this industry?
1. Production of algae-based biofuels is possible in seas only and not on continents.
2. Setting up and engineering the algae-based biofuel production requires a high level of expertise/technology until the construction is completed.
3. Economically viable production necessitates the setting up of large-scale facilities which may raise ecological and social concerns.
Select the correct answer using the code given below:
67.x: Statement 1 is incorrect: Algae cultivation need not be restricted to seas or other marine environments; it can be grown in various water bodies, including ponds, lakes, and artificial tanks on land. Statement 2 is correct: Setting up algae-based biofuel production requires sophisticated engineering and advanced technology, especially during the initial stages of construction. Expertise is essential for designing and constructing facilities that can efficiently cultivate and harvest algae for biofuel. Statement 3 is correct: Large algae farms can consume significant amounts of water, energy, and land, potentially leading to environmental issues such as water scarcity, habitat disruption, or changes in land use. PMF Concept Hack: Statement 1 can be eliminated first because it imposes an absolute geographical restriction ("seas only"), which is scientifically incorrect for algae-based biofuels, since algae can be cultivated in freshwater, wastewater, and controlled land-based systems as well. Such "only/not only" exclusivity is a common UPSC trap. Statement 2 cannot be easily negated because developing and scaling Algae-based biofuels is indeed technology-intensive and requires significant expertise in cultivation, harvesting, and processing. Statement 3 is also broadly valid because economically viable production often demands large-scale infrastructure, which can raise ecological and social concerns due to land use, resource demand, and environmental trade-offs.

Ethanol (C₂H₅OH) is a renewable, flammable, colourless bio-alcohol used as a transport fuel. • Production modes: Produced through fermentation of sugars/starches or by ethylene hydration. • Energy Characteristics: Ethanol has a high-octane rating but is 27% less energy-dense than petrol. • Dual Role: It serves as a petrol additive and as a standalone fuel (E85, E100) in flex-fuel cars. • Non-Fuel Use: Ethanol is also used in sanitisers, perfumes, beverages, and industrial solvents. • By-Products: Distillers' dried grains (DDGS) from grain ethanol are reused as animal feed.

Consider the following materials:
1. Agricultural residues
2. Corn grains
3. Wastewater treatment sludge
4. Wood mill waste
Which of the above can be used as feedstock for producing Sustainable Aviation Fuel?
67.x: All are correct: Also known as Bio-Jet Fuel, Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) is a carbon-reduction solution that is available for use in aircraft and helicopters. It is a "drop-in" fuel that can be blended up to 50% with traditional jet fuel. Its chemical and physical properties are similar to conventional jet fuel. It can be used in existing aircraft engines without modifications and can be blended with conventional jet fuel, making it relatively easy to integrate into existing aviation infrastructure. The feedstocks used for the production of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) include corn grain, oil seeds, algae, agricultural and forestry residues, wood mill waste, municipal solid waste streams, and wet wastes such as animal manures and wastewater treatment sludge. These renewable and waste-derived resources help reduce the aviation sector's dependence on conventional fossil fuels and contribute to lower greenhouse gas emissions.

(a) In form of hydrides (b) In form of water (c) By compressing hydrogen gas (d) None of the above 70th B.P.S.C. (Pre) (Re-Exam) 2024 Ans. (c) Hydrogen can be stored physically as either a compressed gas or a liquid. Compressed hydrogen storage (which is most common) typically involves compressing hydrogen gas into high-pressure cylinders or tanks. The pressure is typically between 350 and 700 bar (around 5,000 and 10,000 psi). This compression increases the density of the hydrogen, allowing it to be stored in a smaller volume. Hydrogen can also be stored in a liquid state at cryogenic temperatures, which are significantly below the boiling point of hydrogen. This requires specialized insulated tanks to maintain the low temperatures. Storage of hydrogen as a liquid requires cryogenic temperatures because the boiling point of hydrogen at one atmosphere pressure is around – 252.9°C. Hydrogen can also be stored on the surfaces of solids (by adsorption) or within solids (by absorption). Cryo-Compressed Hydrogen is a hybrid method that stores hydrogen at cryogenic temperatures while also pressurizing it in a special vessel.
